title: OMOP CDM
text:
Whenever you go to the doctor, or have any medical consultation, the medical professional attending you enters your data in an electronic platform. Think of it as that they will fill in an excel file and upload it to the computer, and then the computer distributes the data to the appropriate table segregated by type (demographics, diagnostics, drugs, procedures…). For example, the doctor might enter “Anne Marie Smith, 46 years old, female, consultation because of respiratory symptoms, fever, flu diagnosis”. Then, your name changes into an anonymized number that represents you without personal information, a “person_id”, and your sociodemographic information (age, sex) will go to the sociodemographic table linked to your person_id. Your clinical information (fever, flu diagnosis) will go to the clinical table linked to your hash, and like this with all the different information that the doctor might add. This set of variables that construct your medical records, are what we call Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) and are the basis of observational medical research.
These data, however, are rarely structured and each healthcare provider might collect it differently. Therefore, when doing a collaborative study, data scientists often encounter difficulties leading with data, since they have to treat differently every site, with independent data pre-processing and analysis pipelines, what makes the study advance slowly and prompt to errors. Imagine your high-school class and that every other classmate would speak a language different to yours; communication and collaboration would not be fluid, right? At one point, researchers from around the world decided that it was worth investing in creating a common language to allow for a more open, reproducible and collaborative science. Nevertheless, like it has happened in human history with languages, several options were raised. English, esperanto, interlingua… In EHR, this translates to OMOP CDM, Sentinel CDM, PCORNet CDM… But we will focus on the language developed by OHDSI and that is accepted by the European Medicaments Agency (EMA): OMOP CDM.
Aligned to the languages example, there is no gold standard CDM, no “better” model. Each one of them is useful and necessary on their own. What differs is, mostly, the dictionary used to map the data. There are some words that have no direct translation to other languages. For example, in Spanish the term “sobremesa” refers to the time spent talking after eating while you are still sitting around the table, and it can extend from 30 minutes to several hours. This term has no translation in English. The same can happen in CDMs. The OMOP CDM uses the standard language SNOMED for most concepts, except for medicines which standard notation is in RxNorm. Other CDMs might use different standards, like using ICD-10 codes to describe diagnoses. The same disease might be diagnosed differently using ICD-10 codes and SNOMED codes, since they have different words for the same concept.


Oftentimes, being specific with your mapping is difficult, since the source data (EHR) might have granular information like “Heart failure of the left atrium with ejection fraction of 20%” but your SNOMED vocabulary will only have “Heart failure”/“Failure of the left heart”/“Reduced ejection fraction”. In this case, how would you map that source diagnosis?


Heart failure TRUEFALSE
Failure of the left heart TRUEFALSE
Reduced ejection fraction TRUEFALSE




Why?

The thing is, that all previous answers are correct, it is just a matter of personal preference or discussing with clinicians what is to prioritise. In the OHDSI tutorials you have some guidance on how to map your data to an OMOP CDM.

For more information about the OMOP CDM, please, refer to: https://ohdsi.github.io/CommonDataModel/

title: OHDSI Journey
text:
The Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (or OHDSI, pronounced “Odyssey”) program is a multi-stakeholder, interdisciplinary collaborative to bring out the value of health data through large-scale analytics. OHDSI has established an international network of researchers and observational health databases with a central coordinating center housed at Columbia University.
The OHDSI mission is to improve health by empowering a community to collaboratively generate the evidence that promotes better health decisions and better care. In OHDSI, and also in GREG (see Why GREG?), we do large scale, multicentre analyses in a federated manner, so that data remains with each data partner and the only thing that is shared is the data format, the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM), as well as analytical tools developed by the OHDSI collaborators and, most recently, by the DARWIN EU® project.
The OHDSI network was built to do collaborative studies to which one can adhere whether they find them interesting or recognise their potential contribution benefits. The OHDSI forums are the standard communication and informative tool, and you can find several nodes of OHDSI to “restrict” your research geographically, for example:

OHDSI Europe
OHDSI Japan
OHDSI Korea
OHDSI China
OHDSI LATAM
OHDSI en Español

But you can also find groups by role (developer, implementer, researcher…) and, of course, a General channel. There are regular meetings to which you are kindly requested to attend, may you have an ongoing project within the OHDSI network.
Read more about OHDSI: https://www.ohdsi.org/

title: Why GREG?
text:
But, if there are already projects like OHDSI, if DARWIN EU ® is already an ongoing project linked to the EMA, why do we need the project GREG?
While OHDSI provides the methodological framework and analytical tools and DARWIN EU® operationalises those tools to answer specific regulatory questions at the EMA level, a critical gap remains: who ensures that the diverse ecosystem of stakeholders, i.e., pharmaceutical companies, medical device manufacturers, HTA bodies, hospital researchers, patient organisations; generates evidence consistently, rigorously, and in a manner that is accepted across the board?






Tip



You should never assume that the same guideline is a gold standard for every stakeholder!


This is the gap that GREG was designed to address. GREG is the acronym for the project name “Testing, improving, and co-creating Guidance and Tools for Real World Evidence Generation and Use for Decision-Making in Europe” . It is a 60-month initiative that began in May 2025, funded by the Innovative Health Initiative Joint Undertaking (IHI JU). Despite the proliferation of guidelines and recommendations for real-world evidence generation, they are not consistently interpreted, applied, or accepted across stakeholder groups. The divergence between regulatory agencies and HTA bodies is a particularly concrete illustration of this problem.






Caution



Let’s take the example of medical devices:

The EMA, as a regulatory body, evaluates the safety and efficacy of a medicine/vaccine/device/drug-device combination; the question it asks is, broadly, does this work and is it safe?
HTA bodies, such as NICE in England, the Haute Autorité de Santé in France, or the G-BA in Germany ask a fundamentally different question: is this better than what we already have, and is it worth the cost?

These are not the same question, and they do not require the same evidence. A medical device manufacturer may successfully obtain CE (European Conformity) marking following EMA-aligned regulatory requirements, only to face entirely different, and sometimes contradictory, evidentiary demands from each national HTA body when seeking reimbursement. The evidence generated for one purpose must then be reframed, supplemented, or entirely duplicated to satisfy another. The requirement for an active comparator arm, and the use of surrogate endpoints are areas where regulators and HTA bodies frequently disagree. Furthermore, while some HTA bodies such as NICE have established frameworks receptive to real-world evidence, many others either lack a formal policy entirely or restrict acceptable evidence to traditional clinical studies, creating a fragmented landscape where the same device, supported by the same data, may be reimbursed in one European country and rejected in another.


GREG aims to address this by generating guidance and tools to advance the use of RWE in the development and evaluation of medicines, medical devices, and drug-device combinations, supporting both regulatory and HTA decision-making. Critically, rather than producing guidance in isolation, the consortium actively engages with regulators, HTA bodies, healthcare professionals, industry partners, and patients to co-design and validate its tools and guidance, with pilot testing studies of relevance and an active dialogue with decision-making bodies planned to support endorsement and alignment, fostering harmonised assessment practices across Europe.
In this context, OHDSI, DARWIN EU®, and GREG are not redundant, but complementary. OHDSI establishes the methodological foundation. DARWIN EU® applies it at the regulatory level and develops its own tools. GREG ensures that the broader European ecosystem has the guidance, tools, and shared understanding necessary to generate evidence that is robust, consistent, and fit for decision-making across all relevant stakeholder contexts.

The OHDSI community wrote the book to serve as a central knowledge repository for all things OHDSI. This book is a great introduction to the OMOP CDM and how to plan and execute studies using OMOP CDM databases and OHDSI tools such as ATLAS or the OHDSI R packages.

title: OMOP CDM
text:
2 Structure
In the Book of OHDSI, you will find everything you need to understand how data is structured in the OMOP CDM. Think of your medical history as a jigsaw puzzle. Each table (conditions, drugs, procedures, measurements, and so on) holds one piece of the picture, recording a different kind of medical or sociodemographic information. On its own, no single piece tells you much. But every piece has a matching edge: your identifying number, or person_id. That shared edge is what lets all the pieces click together into one complete picture: your medical history.
In the Figure below, you can see all the different tables that build up the OMOP CDM, with the different variables that each one records.



Figure. The OMOP CDM 5.4 table structure, including all variables available.








Important



OMOP standardisation enables reproducible observational research across institutions.


Nevertheless, and although all different sites will share the same data structure, it does not mean that they all have the same information recorded. Some sites might have a complete date of birth, while others will only incorporate month and year of birth, due to regional data privacy policies. Some sites will have information on devices, or economic information, some not. This will also depend on which type of data is being mapped: claims data, primary care, hospital care, emergency care… This will make a crucial difference, since some analyses will be restricted by the resolution of the data available in each site or even the data source type.

section: 3 Why studies with observational data are important?
text:
3 Why studies with observational data are important?
At this point, you might wonder, why so much effort? Why is it important to do studies with observational data? Why do we want to guarantee observational data quality and standardisation?
The answer is as complex as it is simple. A medicine, vaccine or device generally cannot be commercialized without a clinical trial proving its effectiveness and assessing its safety. However, clinical trials are costly, usually done with a small sample size of patients, and of limited heterogeneity of the population. It is impossible to design a trial that covers all minority cases. At the same time, would you agree, as a pregnant woman, to undergo a clinical trial? Would you agree your children to undergo one? The answer to these questions is most probably “not if not desperate”.






Note



Observational data allow us to (partially) cover the heterogeneity caveats that clinical trials have.


Clinical trials, especially randomised clinical trials (RCT), are the gold standard to prove the effectiveness and safety of medicinal products and devices. Nevertheless, observational data allow us to ascertain that what we saw in the trial is applicable to the reality of administration of the product, as well as generalisable to all its target populations. Observational data will, at the same time, cover one aspect that is not accounted for in RCTs: off-label prescription. This is when a medicine/device is given to a patient though the medicine/device was not authorised for this purpose. And it is a reality in real-life clinical settings. That is also why observational data is often called real-wor






Important



You can use observational data to study the effectiveness and safety of medicines, vaccines and devices under real-world implementation conditions!


The importance of real-world evidence has not gone unnoticed by regulators. The EMA has been actively working to integrate observational data into regulatory decision-making, with the explicit goal of embedding real-world evidence into its processes by 2025. To operationalise this, EMA and the European Medicines Regulatory Network established the Data Analysis and Real World Interrogation Network (DARWIN EU ®) to provide timely and reliable evidence on the use, safety, and effectiveness of medicines for human use. What makes DARWIN EU® particularly relevant is that they develop and make publicly available statistical tools that work with the OMOP CDM to produce RWE, therefore, the standardisation pipeline that you are learning in this tutorial is not an academic exercise, it is the same infrastructure that feeds into European regulatory decisions. As of 2026, DARWIN EU® has access to data from around 250 million patients, with 108 research topics assessed and 88 studies completed or ongoing.

text:
3 What is my task in GREG?
To answer this question, you need to be aware of which WP you are involved in. Each WP has their own responsibilities and objectives. Please, keep an eye to the Teams channel of your WP and the General GREG channel to make sure that you are up to date with current use cases and work.
Besides, you are expected to attend to the monthly remote meetings of your WP, where you will discuss the ongoing work and you will be able to make suggestions, receive feedback, and collaborate towards your WP objective.






Tip

2.1 Study title
Please, think of a title for your study. Let it start by “GREG -” to make sure that the study is related to the project. As much as possible, a good title should contain at least five elements: the target Population, the Intervention or Exposure of interest, the Comparator, the Outcome of interest, and the Time frame over which the outcome is assessed, commonly referred to by the acronym PICO(T). In the context of observational research, the intervention component is replaced by exposure, giving rise to the PECO framework, because pharmacoepidemiological studies are non-interventional.






Tip



Be concise! A short but informative title is better than a very long and specific title!



Let’s consider the title of our example study “Use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and risk of acute pancreatitis in type 2 diabetes patients”. Is this a good study title? Does it follow the PECO framework? Let’s see:


Population: TRUEFALSE Exposure: TRUEFALSE Comparator: TRUEFALSE Outcome: TRUEFALSE Time: TRUEFALSE


Can you think of a better research question fulfilling all PECO(T) requirements?



2.2 Description of the study team
Who is going to work on this project with you? What will be their responsibilities? Which institution do they work for?


2.3 Milestones
At this stage, the milestones/timelines section is merely speculative. Nevertheless, having to think of realistic timelines for your study will make you more conscious about the amount of work that each stage will take. Remember, that not only you will need to work on the protocol, the analytical code for the study or writing the study report, but you will also need other members of your team to review your work, and each data partner (DP) to individually run the study with the code you (or the Data Scientist of your team) provided. This can take a different amount of time depending on the scale of the database of each DP, as well as the time they can dedicate to the project. Please, consider this when setting your timelines.


2.4 Rationale and background
This section sets the theoretical background to your study. For the abstract or study outline, please, write a short description of the subject of your study, if possible, not longer than one page. For your protocol, add all necessary information, although try to keep it concise and practical. Add relevant references, state-of-the-art research outcomes and a justification of the election of your topic.






Tip



Think of it as: “What makes your study relevant so that we need to select it as a Use Case for GREG? What makes it suitable for GREG?”




2.5 Research question and objectives
A good research question is the foundation of your study. Your RWE will answer only to that research question.






Important



It is not the same to ask: “What is the effectiveness of the flu vaccine?” Than to ask: “What is the effectiveness of the inhaled versus the injected flu vaccine against hospital admission due to flu-related bronchitis in healthy children without prior flu or bronchiolitis diagnosis?”
The more precise we are, the less room we leave for misleading interpretation of our study results.


A structured research question should follow the PECO framework. The ENCePP Guide on Methodological Standards in Pharmacoepidemiology explicitly states that the research question must be clearly defined before the study protocol can be developed, and the ENCePP Checklist for Study Protocols requires researchers to justify why the study is conducted, what specific objectives it addresses, and whether those objectives are formulated in a way that is answerable with the available data1
In recent years, two complementary frameworks have substantially extended the PICO(T) approach:

The estimand framework, formalised in the ICH E9(R1) addendum published in 2019. It introduces the concept of estimand: a precise definition of the treatment effect of interest. An estimand is defined by five attributes: the target population, the treatment or exposure, the variable (endpoint), the population-level summary measure, and the strategies for handling intercurrent events. A good estimand ensures alignment among the study objective, design, data collection, analysis, and interpretation2. It is also the basis of any properly formulated causal research question.






Note



Intercurrent events are events that occur after treatment initiation that affect either the interpretation or the existence of the measurements associated with the clinical question of interest3.


The target trial emulation, introduced by Hernán and Robins in 20164. This framework serves as a guide to best design and analyse observational studies whilst preventing the most common biases, and starts by clearly defining a causal question about an intervention, specifying the protocol of the hypothetical trial that would answer it, and explaining how the observational data will be used to emulate it4,5.






Tip



Read carefully the ICH E9(R1) addendum before designing your study! It might raise questions about what you plan to do that you have not considered before.



Regarding study objectives, make sure that they have a logical order (from general to specific). They need to outline exactly what your research will achieve. Start each with a strong action verb (e.g., evaluate, analyze, compare, determine) and follow the SMART Framework:

Specific: Clearly state what will be done.
Measurable: Identify the main variables you will q uantify.
Achievable: Ensure you can do it with available time and resources.
Relevant: Map directly to your overall research question.
Time-bound: Define the timeframe for the study.

What would be a good research question for our study? (Choose the most complete)

 Among adult patients with type 2 diabetes initiating antidiabetic therapy, what is the time to first acute pancreatitis event comparing new users of GLP-1 receptor agonists versus new users of DPP-4 inhibitors or SGLT-2 inhibitors, using real-world data standardised to the OMOP Common Data Model? Among adult patients with type 2 diabetes initiating any GLP-1 receptor agonist for the first time and no prior pancreatitis-related outcome, what is the comparative risk of acute pancreatitis event comparing semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, and tirzepatide, using each agent as reference in pairwise comparisons, where treatment discontinuation, switching to another GLP-1, or initiation of a concomitant pancreatitis-associated drug are handled as censoring events under a hypothetical strategy? Among adult patients with type 2 diabetes with no prior GLP-1 receptor agonist use, what is the risk of having acute pancreatitis in GLP-1 receptor agonist, over a follow-up period of up to 3 years, under a while-on-treatment strategy?


Notice that the research question makes a big difference on the type of study that you will end up conducting. Are you comparing GLP-1 receptor agonists among them? Or with DPP-4 or SGLT-2 inhibitors? What will be your censoring events? Are you considering new use? Nevertheless, there is not just one good answer, if complete and rigorous, several research questions might be appropriate but they would respond to different study objectives.







Tip



An observational study needs to answer a clinically relevant question. Think of it as an answer to a question that your doctor might ask themselves before prescribing you any treatment: among the treatment options I can give to this patient, which is the safest for them?



As for the objectives, in our study they could be:

Calculate the yearly prevalence and incidence proportion and density of GLP-1 receptor agonists given as a treatment to type 2 diabetes patients.
Characterise the users of each GLP-1 receptor agonists, including sociodemographic, clinical and large-scale characteristics.
Define the mean duration of treatment and treatment patterns, including switches, for patients with type 2 diabetes exposed to GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Assess the comparative safety of the different GLP-1 receptor agonists against acute pancreatitis outcomes.




2.6 Research methods
In this section, you need to describe the methodology that you will do to successfully pursue your study. Our aim is to do open, transparent, reproducible science. Be specific, be rigorous, do not let anything for imagination or speculation.






Tip



When writing the methods section, try to think “Would someone from a different study team be able to execute the same study as my team?”



2.6.1 Study design
To decide your study design, you need to bear in mind your study objectives. Do you want to do a characterisation study? Drug utilisation? Incidence/prevalence? Or are you going to answer a causal question? All of these might need different study designs.



Figure. Scheme of some study designs.


In the ENCePP Guide on Methodological Standards in Pharmacoepidemiology you will find a description of the most common study designs used to generate RWE. Most of the times, you will do a cohort study design for characterisation, and an active comparator, target trial emulation for causal inference. Nevertheless, even these designs can be further specified, for example explicitly stating whether you will use a new-user or prevalent-user approach.

For our GLP-1 comparative risk of pancreatitis study, a good study design could be:
- New user cohort study (for characterisation)
- New user, active comparator, target trial emulation study (for safety assessment)



2.6.2 Study period
The study period is the time between the start of your study and its end. Avoid unnecessary large study periods: what length is sufficient to ascertain your hypothesis? Also, take into account the dates in which the different products you study (or the outcomes) started to be available. For example, it does not make sense to make a study of causal inference related to COVID-19 with study period starting before 2019.

For our GLP-1 comparative risk of pancreatitis study, we will be comparing semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, and tirzepatide among each other. Tirzepatide was only approved by the EMA on September 2022. Therefore, a good study period could be January 1st, 2023 to December 31st, 2025 or the most recent data available in each database.







Caution



This would, however, raise a limitation: you can only say that you studied the comparative safety of GLP-1 use for 3 years. You cannot state that your study results are applicable to a longer-term safety.




2.6.3 Study population
In this section, consider all relevant sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of your population. Their age, sex, whether you want to study a particular socioeconomic stratum or ethnic, whether you need your population to have a previous condition or not.

In our example, we will need two populations:
General population (Population A): All adults (≥18 years) with a recorded diagnosis of type 2 diabetes who are actively registered in the participating database and eligible for observation during each calendar year of the study period (1st January 2023 to 31st December 2025, or the latest data available). Eligible individuals must have at least 365 days of continuous observation before index date. Individuals must have continuous database enrollment or observation for the period required to contribute person-time. This is the population “at risk” of receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists, it serves as the denominator for annual prevalence and incidence estimates of GLP-1 receptor agonist use. If they receive the treatment, they are censored from this population, but for each type of GLP-1. For example, if they receive semaglutide, they are no longer in population A for incidence or prevalence of semaglutide calculation, but they remain in population A for dulaglutide-related calculations.
New-user population (Population B): Adults (≥18 years) with type 2 diabetes who initiate treatment with one of the study GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, or tirzepatide) for the first time during the study period. Eligible individuals must have at least 365 days of continuous observation before treatment initiation, no dispensing or prescription of any GLP-1 receptor agonist during the washout period, and no recorded history of acute pancreatitis or related outcomes before the index date. The date of first dispensing or prescription defines cohort entry (index date). Patients contribute only their first eligible treatment episode for each type of GLP-1 receptor agonist. That means, that the same patient might be part of the semaglutide and liraglutide cohorts, but just once for each cohort.



2.6.4 Follow-up
To define the follow-up of your population of study, the HARPER guidelines are a basic. You must define the index date of your study without introducing immortal time bias, and set your censoring events wisely. HARPER diagrams help with visualisation. Have a look at: https://doi.org/10.1002/pds.5507
Each of your populations might have different follow-up definitions.

In our example, there are two different follow-up definitions, one for each population:

Population A: they will contribute observation time from the date they satisfy the eligibility criteria (diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, age ≥18 years, prior observation of 365 days) within the study period. Follow-up will continue until the earliest of death, transfer out of the database, end of continuous observation, or prescription of a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Individuals may contribute person-time to more than one calendar year provided they remain eligible. This dynamic cohort will serve as the denominator for estimating the annual prevalence and incidence of GLP-1 receptor agonist use.




Figure. HARPER diagram for population A in our example.



Population B: they will contribute observation time beginning on the index date, defined as the date of the first prescription or dispensing of a GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, or tirzepatide) during the study period (1st January 2023 to 31st December 2025, or the latest available date in each database), after satisfying all eligibility criteria. Participants will be followed from treatment initiation until the earliest occurrence of an acute pancreatitis event (study outcome), discontinuation of the index GLP-1 receptor agonist, switching to another GLP-1 receptor agonist, initiation of a concomitant medication associated with pancreatitis risk, death, loss to follow-up or end of data availability, or end of the study period, whichever occurs first. Treatment discontinuation, switching to another GLP-1 receptor agonist, and initiation of a concomitant pancreatitis-associated medication will be treated as censoring events.



Figure. HARPER diagram for population B in our example.






2.6.5 Variables
You should consider all the variables that are relevant to define the eligibility of your population (age, sex, year, region, clinical diagnoses, measurements…), as well as those that are relevant for the study (exposure, outcomes, confounders, stratification variables…). You can introduce covariables, like concomitant medication or comorbidities. It can be a good approach to search for the published literature or similar studies in the EMA Catalogue to explore the variables that have been previously used in related analyses.


2.6.6 Sample size
If you are doing a characterisation study, sample size calculation is not applicable. You can say that you are using information from all patients available in the corresponding databases, and provide some counts on the number of patients of each database, if relevant. For effectiveness and safety studies, you should provide a calculation of estimated sample size needed to observe an effect.
To do a sample size calculation, you need to define your statistical test, set your acceptable error margins (typically α=0.05, power =0.80), and estimate the effect size (the difference you expect to find between cohorts). These parameters are then plugged into formulas or software to determine the required participant count. Some of these variables might be obtained from published literature, like previous incidence or prevalence of disease before intervention (e.g. for vaccines) or the expected effect of the intervention or treatment (from clinical studies or previous observational studies).


2.6.7 Analysis
This is the core of the study for the data analyst of your team. Defining well the analysis section will ascertain reproducibility of the study if the analytical code is lost for whatever reason. In the Study design & execution section of this tutorial, you will find examples of implementation of different types of studies.
Nevertheless, for further information, you can look at:

The Book of OHDSI
What if…?
Developing a Protocol for Observational Comparative Effectiveness Research: A User’s Guide
OHDSI R packages
DARWIN EU packages

But also check the tutorials in:

EHDEN Academy

title: Standard Procedure
text:
The feasibility of your UC proposal will already be explored before the UCPTF. From your study outline, WP6 will gather the relevant information for a first-step feasibility exploration of resources and methods (in collaboration with WP4 and WP5) to inform the UCPTF before proceeding with a UC.
Once a UC is prioritised, the first proper feasibility assessment, named landscaping, includes:

Potential database information: national/regional, primary care/secondary care, etc.
Codelist with 40 concept ids: an Excel file with ~40 concept ids that will be relevant for your study. Tools that will help you build this codelist are Athena and ATLAS, that will be better explained in the ATLAS section.
With this landscaping, data partners will be selected among the GREG consortium, the EHDEN portal or other particularly relevant data holders.

Once your study is already ongoing and you are finishing the study protocol, you will need to prepare for the final feasibility exploration report. You will need to define up to 5 different phenotypes for your study’s feasibility assessment (see Phenotyping section). Please, notice that these phenotypes do not necessarily need to be the same as the cohorts that you will create for your study. These 5 phenotypes will be run in the available databases, selected from landscaping. Counts for all different concept ids included in your phenotypes’ concept sets, will be reported in an exploration report, along with attrition tables.

Once you have the exploration report with feasibility results, you can select up to 10 databases for your study. This is the step when data partners are hired to join the project.






Note



Please, provide a rule or quantitative way (score) for deciding your final 10 databases. You will need to justify your choices.










Tip



You can always ask WP6 (Lucia C. and Lucia B.) to assist you with your choices or phenotype development!

title: ATLAS
text:
3 Brief introduction to ATLAS
ATLAS is organised around a left-hand navigation panel with several modules, each corresponding to a distinct analytical task. Here you will find a brief description of the five modules you will use most frequently in a GREG study: Concept Sets, Cohort Definitions, Characterisation, Incidence Rates, and Effectiveness estimation.

3.1 Concept Sets
Everything in ATLAS starts with a concept set. A concept set is a reusable, named collection of OMOP standard concept ids that together represent a clinical entity, such as a disease, a drug, a procedure or a measurement. Before you can define a cohort, you need to define the concepts that describe it.
To build a concept set, you use the search module to query the OMOP vocabulary, and then add relevant concepts to a concept set. You can use Athena for assistance, see Support with Athena. An important decision at this stage is whether to include descendants: ticking the Include Descendants checkbox means that all more-specific child concepts in the SNOMED or RxNorm hierarchy are automatically included, which is usually desirable for conditions and drug ingredients.

For the GLP-1 receptor agonist vs. acute pancreatitis study, we need at minimum three concept sets:

GLP-1 receptor agonists: built by searching for each ingredient (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, tirzepatide) in the RxNorm vocabulary and including descendants to capture all branded formulations and dose forms automatically.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus: built using relevant SNOMED concepts for type 2 diabetes mellitus with descendants included, to capture all coded sub-types.
Acute pancreatitis: built using relevant SNOMED concepts for acute pancreatitis with descendants included, restricted to inpatient or emergency settings to improve specificity, or we could even include drug exposure concepts related to some treatment for acute pancreatitis as a proxy for the diagnosis.








Tip



When you add a concept and tick Include Descendants, ATLAS shows you the Descendant Person Count (DPC): the number of patients in the connected database who have at least one record mapped to that concept or any of its descendants. A DPC of zero usually means the concept is not used in your data, either because it is not coded or because the data source does not capture it. Always review this before finalising your concept set.


Quick check: In ATLAS, you are building the concept set for semaglutide. You search for ‘semaglutide’ and find the RxNorm ingredient concept. Should you tick Include Descendants?
TRUEFALSE


Why?

Ticking Include Descendants ensures that all branded products and dose forms are captured automatically. If you only include the ingredient-level concept without descendants, you will miss every prescription recorded at the product level, which is how most EHR and claims data are coded.

Quick check: In ATLAS, you are building the concept set for acute pancreatitis. You search for ‘pancreatitis’ and find the SNOMED concept. You tick Include Descendants because this is the standard approach. Have you successfully built the concept set for acute pancreatitis?
TRUEFALSE


Why?

No. Ticking Include Descendants does not make your concept set correct immediately. Since you are including all pancreatitis with descendants, you are also incorporating to your concept set chronic pancreatitis, surgery-derived pancreatitis, and others. You should be specific when building your concept set!


3.1.1 Example of acute pancreatitis:







Figure. Acute pancreatitis concept set building with ATLAS.






3.2 Cohort definitions
A cohort in ATLAS is a set of persons who satisfy one or more inclusion criteria to be your population of study for a defined duration of time. Every cohort has:

An entry event: the clinical event that marks the start of the cohort period (index date)
Inclusion criteria: additional conditions that must be met at or before the index date
Cohort exit: the event or rule that determines when a person leaves the cohort

Cohort definitions in ATLAS are built using a drag-and-drop interface that translates directly into SQL executed against your OMOP database. Once saved, a cohort definition can be reused across all analytical modules, shared with collaborators across the network, and exported as JSON for version control and to be analysed in R (see The Book of OHDSI).

In our study, we will define five separate exposure cohorts, one per GLP-1 RA agent. Nevertheless, for this example, we will consider them all together for simplicity:

Entry event: first prescription (drug exposure start date) for the agent of interest, using the corresponding concept set built in the previous step.
Inclusion criteria:

Age ≥ 18 years at index date
Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus at any time prior to or on the index date (using the diabetes concept set)
No prior prescription of the specific GLP-1 of interest in the 365 days before the index date (washout window to enforce the new-user design)
At least 365 days of continuous observation prior to the index date (to ensure adequate baseline covariate capture)

Cohort exit: the earliest of treatment discontinuation, switch to another GLP-1 RA, acute pancreatitis or initiation of a pancreatitis-associated drug, death, or end of observation.








Important



A concept set is just a list of concept IDs, it has no temporal logic and no patient-level criteria. A cohort uses concept sets as building blocks but adds the when, the how long, and the who else qualifies. You can think of concept sets as vocabulary and cohorts as grammar.

Tip

This produces incidence rates, attrition tables, time distributions, and index event breakdown plots that allow you to detect errors in your cohort logic. We will discuss how to implement this in R in the Diagnostics section of this tutorial.






3.3 Characterisation
The Characterisation module allows you to describe the baseline characteristics of one or more cohorts, including demographics, comorbidities, concomitant medications, prior procedures, and measurements, as prevalence and mean values across the cohort at the index date. ATLAS comes with nearly 100 preset feature analyses that perform aggregation and summarisation functions on clinical observations for selected target cohorts, providing potentially thousands of features to describe the cohort’s baseline and post-index characteristics.
Characterisation is useful for two distinct purposes in a study:

Before the analysis, to understand who is in each cohort and whether the study population makes clinical sense.
After propensity score adjustment, to compare covariate balance between exposure groups before and after adjustment, using the standardised mean difference (SMD). An SMD below 0.1 for all covariates is generally considered indicative of adequate balance.


Imagine that we run Characterisation in our example study.

You run the characterisation and notice that the prevalence of prior hypertriglyceridaemia is 18% in the semaglutide cohort but 31% in the exenatide cohort. What should you do?
Ignore it, because small differences in baseline characteristics are expectedInclude hypertriglyceridaemia as a covariate in the propensity score model to adjust for this imbalanceExclude all patients with hypertriglyceridaemia from both cohortsRe-define the semaglutide cohort to match the exenatide cohort prevalence


Why?

Hypertriglyceridaemia is an established independent risk factor for acute pancreatitis and is differentially distributed between your exposure groups. This is precisely the definition of a confounder. The correct action is to include it in the propensity score model (or as a covariate in the outcome model) so that the hazard ratio comparing the two agents is not distorted by this baseline difference. Excluding patients or re-defining cohorts based on observed imbalances would introduce selection bias and change your target population.




3.4 Incidence Rates
The Incidence Rates module estimates the crude incidence rate (or incidence proportion) of an outcome within one or more target cohorts, stratified by calendar time, age, sex, or any combination thereof. It answers the descriptive question: how often does the outcome occur in this population, per unit of person-time?
This is not a causal analysis but it is a crucial first step in any study for two reasons: it tells you whether your outcome cohort is capturing events at a plausible rate, and it provides the absolute risk context that HR estimates alone cannot convey.

In our example study of type 2 diabetes mellitus users of GLP-1 receptor agonists, we estimate the crude incidence rate of acute pancreatitis within each of the five GLP-1 cohorts, stratified by:

Calendar year (2023, 2024, 2025), to detect any secular trends or data artefacts
Age group, since pancreatitis risk increases with age
Sex, to understand baseline differences

Since the expected background incidence of acute pancreatitis in a type 2 diabetes population is approximately 2-5 per 1,000 person-years, if your crude rates are an order of magnitude higher or lower, this is a signal to revisit the outcome concept set or cohort exit criteria before proceeding to the causal analysis.







Tip



If your incidence rate shows a dramatic spike in a specific calendar year with no clinical explanation, this is almost certainly a data artefact. For example, there could have been a change in coding practice at a data partner, or a batch upload of historical records. Flag this before running the estimation analysis.





3.5 Estimation module
The Estimation module is where the causal analysis takes place. It implements a new-user active-comparator cohort design with propensity score adjustment, and produces the hazard ratio (or other effect measure) comparing the outcome risk between two exposure cohorts.
The key components of a Cohort Method analysis in ATLAS are:

Target and comparator cohorts: the two exposure groups being compared (e.g. semaglutide vs. liraglutide)
Outcome cohort: the event of interest (acute pancreatitis)
Covariates: features extracted from the baseline window to build the propensity score; ATLAS allows you to select from the same preset feature analyses used in characterisation
Propensity score model: ATLAS uses LASSO logistic regression by default to estimate the probability of treatment assignment given baseline covariates
Analysis settings: trimming (e.g. remove top 1% of propensity scores), matching or weighting strategy (1:1 matching, variable ratio matching, IPTW), and outcome model (Cox proportional hazards regression)
Negative controls: a set of outcome concepts where no true causal effect is expected, used to detect and calibrate for residual systematic error (unmeasured confounding, outcome misclassification, immortal time)


Because we are comparing five agents in our example study, we run a series of pairwise comparisons (semaglutide vs. liraglutide, semaglutide vs. dulaglutide, semaglutide vs. exenatide, and so on) each as a separate Cohort Method analysis. For each pair:

Propensity scores should be estimated using demographic, comorbidity, and medication covariates from the 365 days prior to the index date
Cohorts should be trimmed to the region of common support (patients with extreme propensity scores who have no plausible counterpart in the other group are excluded)
Cohorts should be exactly matched 1:1 on the propensity score in first instance. If we lose a lot of sample size then we can consider other configurations.
A Cox proportional hazards model should be fitted on the matched sample, with time zero at the index date and time-to-first acute pancreatitis event as the outcome
A set of 50-100 negative control outcomes should be included to assess and calibrate residual bias

The primary output is a calibrated hazard ratio with 95% confidence interval and empirical p-value for each pairwise comparison.







Note



A negative control outcome is a condition that the exposure is not believed to cause. For instance, “ingrown toenail” or “broken wrist” as outcomes in a drug safety study. If your analysis finds a hazard ratio different from 1.0 for negative controls, this is evidence of systematic error (bias) in your analysis pipeline that is not explained by the drugs themselves. ATLAS uses the distribution of negative control estimates to empirically calibrate your p-values and confidence intervals, producing estimates that are honest about the true uncertainty in the analysis. This is now considered best practice in OHDSI network studies.

2 Installation

2.1 Installing R and RStudio
Please, check this guide: https://ohdsi.github.io/Hades/rSetup.html


2.2 Setting up R
Ideally, when you are doing R code for a GREG study, you will create a new R project and set up the environment. This includes installing all the packages required for the project and recording the package versions in a .lock file. By doing so, you can restore the exact same environment whenever you open the project in a new session or on a different computer, ensuring that the code remains reproducible and consistent over time.
A common workflow is to use the renv package, which creates an isolated project library and manages package dependencies. After installing the required packages, you can save the environment with renv::snapshot(), which generates the renv.lock file. Later, anyone working on the project can recreate the same environment by running renv::restore(). This approach minimizes compatibility issues caused by package updates and helps guarantee that analyses can be reproduced exactly as originally performed.
Install all packages you will need for these tutorials and set up the environment:


Code
install.packages("renv")

renv::init()

install.packages(c(
  "CDMConnector",
  "omopgenerics",
  "omock",
  "PhenotypeR",
  "CodelistGenerator",
  "CohortConstructor",
  "CohortCharacteristics",
  "IncidencePrevalence",
  "DrugUtilisation",
  "CohortSurvival",
  "CohortMethod",
  "dplyr",
  "duckdb",
  "DBI",
  "ggplot2"
))

renv::snapshot()


Later, when you (or someone else) open the project on a different computer or in a fresh R session, simply run:


Code
renv::restore()








Tip



A good practice is to include the following commands at the beginning of your project setup script:


Code
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Project setup
# ------------------------------------------------------------

# Install renv if it is not available
if (!requireNamespace("renv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("renv")
}

# Restore the project environment
renv::activate()
renv::restore()


But! Notice that some databases might not be connected to the internet and therefore you will not be able to recover the environment with these commands. In that case, you will need to manually install all packages required for the study!


Code
# If the package is in a local folder:
install.packages("C:/path to folder with the package", 
                 repos = NULL, 
                 type = "source")










Caution



Always remember to load all installed packages necessary for your project with the “library” command!


Code
library(CDMConnector)
library(omopgenerics)
library(omock)
library(CohortDiagnostics)
library(PhenotypeR)
library(CodelistGenerator)
# [...]






2.3 Working on GitHub
To make the project easier to share, collaborate on, and keep track of changes, it is recommended to use GitHub as a version-control platform. The first step is to create a new repository on GitHub. A repository acts as the central location where all project files, scripts, documentation, and version history are stored.
To create a new repository, log in to your GitHub account, select New repository, choose a descriptive name for the project, and initialize it with a README file if desired. Once the repository has been created, clone it to your local computer using either Git or the GitHub interface. The local copy of the repository will contain all project files and will be connected to the remote GitHub repository.






Tip



You can use GitHub Desktop, it is very convenient!


After cloning the repository, open the project directly from the local folder in RStudio by selecting File → New Project → Existing Directory and choosing the repository folder. This creates an R project (.Rproj) inside the GitHub repository, allowing RStudio to recognize the project structure and keep all files organized.
Once the project is set up, changes can be tracked using Git. After modifying files or adding new scripts, commit the changes with a meaningful message and push them to GitHub. This workflow ensures that the project history is preserved and that collaborators can access the most recent version of the analysis.
For reproducible research, the GitHub repository should include the R project file, the analysis scripts, documentation files, and the renv.lock file created with renv::snapshot(). The renv.lock file allows collaborators to recreate the exact R environment required to run the project.

3 Connecting to an OMOP CDM
With all set up, let’s enter the OMOPverse! To all OMOP analyses, the entrance door is the CDM reference, an R object that represents your database connection and knows where your OMOP tables live (see OMOP CDM). This object in R is created with CDMConnector. You can either work with a real database or synthetic data. If you have access to a real database, you can connect to that one. Nevertheless, some analyses might be very computationally expensive and spend days running.






Tip



You might want to use synthetic data to try your code before running it on real data!



3.1 A. Real database (e.g. PostgreSQL)

library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

# 1. Create a database connection

# 1.1 Database metadata and connection details -----

# name of the database, use acronym in capital letters 
dbName <-

# 1.2 parameters to connect to create cdm object ----

# name of the schema where cdm tables are located
cdmSchema <- "cdm"
 
# name of a schema in the database where you have writing permission
writeSchema <- 

# name of the achilles schema

# combination of at least 5 letters + _ (eg. "abcde_") that will lead any table
# written in the write schema

# connection
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), # Go to: https://dbi.r-dbi.org/
                      host = db_host,
                      port = db_port,
                      dbname = db_cdmvers,
                      user = db_user,
                      password = db_password)

cdm <- cdmFromCon(con = con,
                  cdmSchema = cdmSchema,

Use usethis::edit_r_environ() to open your .Renviron file and store connection credentials there. This prevents accidentally committing passwords to Git and makes your code portable across team members.

For all code examples in these chapters, we use synthetic data generated by the omock package. This means you can run every code block yourself, right now, without needing a real database connection. You can also do this when planning a study, to avoid running unnecessary long codes or codes with bugs in real databases.


Code

# Create a synthetic CDM with 1000 people

  omock::mockPerson(nPerson = 1000) |>
  omock::mockObservationPeriod() |>
  omock::mockConditionOccurrence() |>
  omock::mockDrugExposure() |>
  omock::mockDeath()

# With Eunomia

title: CDM using R
text:
4 Exploring the CDM structure
Once you have a CDM reference, you can inspect it like a named list. Each element is a lazy database table, it does not load data into memory until you explicitly collect() it.


Code
# List all available tables
names(cdm)

# Inspect the person table
cdm$person |> glimpse()

# Count rows without loading everything into memory
cdm$person |> count()

# Look at a few drug exposure records
cdm$drug_exposure |> head(10) |> 
  collect() # At this moment is when we actually retrieve the data!








Note



When you write cdm$drug_exposure |> filter(drug_concept_id == 1503297), R does not immediately execute this against the database. Instead, it builds a query that is only sent to the database when you call collect(), count(), glimpse(), or a summarise* function. This means you can build complex multi-step queries without pulling millions of rows into memory.




Code
# This builds a query but does NOT run it yet
query <- cdm$condition_occurrence |>
  filter(condition_concept_id == 201826) |>  # Type 2 diabetes
  select(person_id, condition_start_date)

# This sends the query to the database and returns results
query |> collect() |> head(5)

5 The omopgenerics result format
All OMOPverse analytical functions return results in a standardised summarised_result format: a tibble with a consistent set of columns regardless of which analysis was run. Understanding this format is essential because all downstream table and plot functions expect it.

title: Phenotyping
text:
A phenotype in biology refers to the observable characteristics of an organism, as opposed to the genotype, which is the underlying genetic blueprint. In the context of observational health data, the term has been adopted with an analogous meaning: a phenotype is a specification of an observable, potentially changing clinical state of a patient, inferred from EHR data, claims data, or other routinely collected health data.
In practice, when we talk about phenotyping in an OMOP study, we mean the process of algorithmically identifying patients who have a particular condition, who received a particular treatment, or who experienced a particular outcome. This is done based on the diagnostic codes, prescriptions, measurements, and clinical notes recorded in their data.






Caution



A phenotype is not a direct observation of clinical reality, but a computational inference about clinical reality based on whatever was recorded in the database!


This distinction matters. A patient coded as having type 2 diabetes mellitus in an EHR may have been coded that way because a clinician confirmed the diagnosis after laboratory testing, because a coding clerk assigned a default code, or because the diagnosis was carried forward from a previous admission without review. The code is the same in all three cases but the clinical reality is not. Phenotyping is the discipline of navigating this uncertainty systematically. In OMOP studies, phenotyping applies to all three core building blocks of a cohort study: the exposure (who received the drug?), the outcome (who experienced the event?), and the population (who has the condition of interest?). You will need to consider all of these elements when building the phenotype for your population of interest, and it is essential that you consider all the domains in which the exposure or outcome that you want to describe might be captured in a relevant way for your study. Do you want to include the concept hyperglycemia in your diabetes study? Then, you might need conditions (hyperglycemia due to type 2 diabetes mellitus) as well as measurements (blood glucose) or observations.






Important



Remember: In the feasibility stage, you will need to provide up to 5 phenotypes. You can ask for help to WP6 in case you need it, both for clinical and programming assistance, since you will need to think of the clinical, sociodemographic, etc. characteristics that your population might have, as well as how to implement it with ATLAS (see the ATLAS section) or CohortConstructor (see the Cohort construction section).
