title: Phenotyping
text:
2 Rule-based vs. probabilistic phenotyping
There are two broad approaches to phenotyping in observational research, and understanding the difference is essential before you choose your tools.

2.1 Rule-based phenotyping
Rule-based phenotyping defines the presence of a clinical state using deterministic logical rules applied to coded data. The most common form is a cohort definition in ATLAS: a patient is included if they have at least one record of a specific concept (or concept set) in a specific domain, within a specified time window, optionally combined with additional inclusion or exclusion criteria.
Rule-based phenotypes are transparent, reproducible, and computationally efficient. Their limitation is that they treat the classification as binary and deterministic — a patient either meets the criteria or does not — which can be overly rigid when the underlying signal in the data is noisy or incomplete.

Our study — rule-based phenotypes for all three components:

Exposure phenotype (GLP-1 RA initiation): at least one drug exposure record for a GLP-1 RA concept, with no prior GLP-1 RA in the preceding 365 days. Rule-based, applied separately for each of the five agents.
Population phenotype (type 2 diabetes): at least one condition occurrence record for a T2DM concept (SNOMED 201826 with descendants) at any time on or before the index date, with no record of type 1 diabetes at any time (exclusion criterion).
Outcome phenotype (acute pancreatitis): at least one condition occurrence record for acute pancreatitis (SNOMED 197456 with descendants) in an inpatient or emergency care setting, occurring after the index date. The restriction to inpatient/emergency visits improves specificity — acute pancreatitis coded in an outpatient setting is more likely to be a chronic or historical coding than a true new event.




2.2 Probabilistic phenotyping
Probabilistic phenotyping, by contrast, produces a predicted probability that each patient in a database has the clinical state of interest, rather than a binary yes/no classification. It uses machine learning models trained on patients who are extremely likely to be true positives (the xSpec cohort — extremely specific) and applied to a large random sample of the database population. The output is a probability score for every patient, which can then be used to evaluate how well a rule-based definition performs.
The main OHDSI tool for probabilistic phenotyping is PheValuator, described in detail below.






TipWhen to use each approach



For most GREG network studies, rule-based phenotyping (ATLAS cohort definitions) is the primary approach — it is fast, interpretable, and can be executed across all network partners without sharing patient-level data. Probabilistic phenotyping with PheValuator is used to evaluate those rule-based definitions: it tells you how sensitive and specific your cohort definition is, which informs whether your study is likely to suffer from misclassification bias.

title: Phenotyping
text:
3 Sensitivity and specificity in phenotyping
When we evaluate a phenotype algorithm, we are essentially asking: of all the patients in the database who truly have the condition, how many does our algorithm correctly identify (sensitivity)? And of all the patients our algorithm flags, how many truly have the condition (positive predictive value / specificity)?
These two properties pull in opposite directions, and the right trade-off depends on the study type:








Study type
Priority
Rationale




Incidence / prevalence
High sensitivity
Better to capture all cases, even if some are false positives


Safety outcome (rare event)
High specificity (PPV)
A false positive outcome event can create a spurious safety signal


Exposure definition
High specificity
Misclassifying non-users as users is a major source of confounding


Characterisation
Balanced
Describes the cohort as captured; misclassification affects interpretation




Our study — why specificity matters more for the outcome: Acute pancreatitis is a serious adverse event with a relatively low background incidence (~2–5 per 1,000 person-years in T2DM patients). A low-specificity outcome phenotype — one that captures chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits, pancreatitis history codes, or rule-out diagnoses coded as confirmatory — would inflate the event count and potentially dilute or distort the hazard ratio. For this reason, restricting the outcome to inpatient or emergency settings is a deliberate specificity-improving decision, even at the cost of some sensitivity.

Quick check: You are designing the outcome phenotype for acute pancreatitis. You have two options: (A) any condition occurrence record for acute pancreatitis in any care setting, or (B) at least one inpatient or emergency acute pancreatitis record. Which has higher specificity?
Option B — inpatient/emergency onlyOption A — any care settingThey have the same specificityIt depends on the database


Explanation

Option B has higher specificity because restricting to inpatient or emergency settings filters out the codes most likely to represent historical diagnoses, follow-up visits for previously diagnosed pancreatitis, or diagnostic uncertainty (where a clinician codes a rule-out condition). Outpatient acute pancreatitis codes are far more likely to be false positives than inpatient codes, where the diagnosis typically requires clinical examination, laboratory findings (lipase/amylase), and often imaging confirmation. The trade-off is reduced sensitivity — some true acute pancreatitis events managed in outpatient settings will be missed — but for a rare serious adverse event, this trade-off is generally acceptable.

title: Phenotyping
section: 4 Tools for phenotyping in the OHDSI ecosystem
text:
4 Tools for phenotyping in the OHDSI ecosystem
The OHDSI ecosystem provides a structured, layered set of tools that cover the full phenotyping workflow — from building concept sets and cohort definitions, to diagnosing their performance, to formally evaluating their sensitivity and specificity, to sharing validated definitions with the global community.

4.1 1. ATLAS — building the phenotype
As covered in the previous chapter, ATLAS is where you build your concept sets and cohort definitions. It is the starting point of every phenotyping workflow. The cohort definition is the phenotype algorithm in its executable form — a JSON specification that can be run against any OMOP CDM database.
The key decisions at this stage are:

Which concept(s) to use and whether to include descendants
Which OMOP domain(s) to search (condition occurrence, drug exposure, measurement, etc.)
What temporal logic to apply (first ever occurrence, any occurrence, occurrence within a window)
What additional inclusion and exclusion criteria to apply







TipCheck the OHDSI Phenotype Library before building from scratch



Before designing a phenotype from scratch, always search the OHDSI Phenotype Library — a publicly accessible, version-controlled catalogue of peer-reviewed cohort definitions contributed by the OHDSI community. It follows FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reproducible) and each entry includes clinical descriptions, technical logic, evaluation results, and a stable DOI. If a validated phenotype for your condition already exists there, reusing it is strongly preferable to building a new one — it saves time and ensures comparability with prior work.




4.2 2. CohortDiagnostics — diagnosing the phenotype
CohortDiagnostics is an R package (part of the HADES ecosystem) that produces a standardised battery of diagnostics for any ATLAS cohort definition, without sharing patient-level data. It is the essential next step after building a cohort in ATLAS and before running any analysis.
The diagnostics it produces include:

Incidence rate of cohort entry over calendar time — a spike or drop in a specific year can indicate a data artefact
Attrition table — how many patients are excluded by each inclusion criterion, helping identify criteria that are too restrictive or too loose
Index event breakdown — which specific concepts are driving cohort entry (e.g. which SNOMED codes are most common at the index date)
Time distribution — the distribution of observation time before and after the index date
Prevalence of covariates before and after the index date — which conditions, drugs, and procedures co-occur with cohort entry

Results are visualised in an interactive Shiny application and can be shared across network partners, making CohortDiagnostics the standard tool for federated phenotype evaluation in DARWIN EU® and OHDSI network studies.

Our study — running CohortDiagnostics on the T2DM and acute pancreatitis cohorts:
Before running the main analysis, we execute CohortDiagnostics on all seven cohorts (five exposure cohorts, one T2DM population cohort, one acute pancreatitis outcome cohort) at each data partner. Key things to look for:

Does the incidence of new GLP-1 RA users increase from 2023 onwards, as expected given tirzepatide’s recent approval?
Is the acute pancreatitis incidence rate in the expected range of 2–5 per 1,000 person-years in the T2DM population?
Does the index event breakdown for the AP outcome cohort show that the majority of entries are driven by inpatient codes? If a large proportion come from outpatient settings despite our restriction, this suggests the care setting mapping may differ between data sources.


Quick check: CohortDiagnostics shows a sharp spike in new GLP-1 RA users in January 2024 at one data partner, but not at any other. What is the most likely explanation?
A genuine increase in GLP-1 RA prescribing at that site in January 2024A data artefact — likely a batch upload of historical records or a change in coding practice at that data partnerA difference in the patient population at that siteThe concept set is too broad and is capturing a different drug class at that site


Explanation

A spike limited to a single data partner and a single time point is almost never a true clinical phenomenon — it is almost always a data artefact. The most common causes are: a batch upload of historical prescription records that were entered into the system with the upload date rather than the original prescription date; a change in the data extraction or ETL (extract-transform-load) pipeline; or a change in coding practice at that site. Before proceeding with the analysis, this anomaly must be investigated with the data partner and either corrected or handled (e.g. by using only the period after the artefact, or by excluding that partner from the primary analysis).



4.3 3. PheValuator — formally evaluating sensitivity and specificity
PheValuator is an R package that provides a semi-automated method for estimating the sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) of a phenotype algorithm — without requiring manual chart review. It does this by building a diagnostic prediction model using a cohort of patients very likely to be true positives (the xSpec — extremely specific cohort, defined by requiring multiple diagnostic codes over time) and applying it to a large random sample of the database to generate a predicted probability of the condition for every patient. These probabilities are then used as a probabilistic gold standard against which the rule-based phenotype algorithm is evaluated.
The key outputs of PheValuator are:

Sensitivity — the proportion of true cases captured by the phenotype algorithm
Specificity — the proportion of true non-cases correctly excluded
PPV — the proportion of algorithm-identified cases that are true cases
NPV — the proportion of algorithm-excluded patients that are true non-cases


Our study — evaluating the T2DM phenotype with PheValuator: The T2DM population phenotype (any T2DM code ever, no T1DM exclusion applied yet) is evaluated using PheValuator. An xSpec cohort is built by requiring at least two T2DM diagnosis codes on separate dates in the 21 days prior to a clinical visit, with no T1DM codes ever recorded. PheValuator builds a prediction model using this xSpec cohort and applies it to a random sample of the full database. The resulting sensitivity and PPV estimates tell us how well our rule-based T2DM cohort definition is actually performing — and whether adding the T1DM exclusion criterion meaningfully improves PPV without sacrificing too much sensitivity.



4.4 4. The OHDSI Phenotype Library — sharing and reusing validated phenotypes
The OHDSI Phenotype Library is the community’s shared repository of cohort definitions, subject to version control, open peer review, and regular quality checks across the OHDSI network. Each entry includes not only the cohort definition JSON but also clinical descriptions, evaluation results from CohortDiagnostics and PheValuator, contributor attribution, and a stable DOI that can be cited in publications.
For GREG studies, consulting the Phenotype Library before developing new definitions is both a time-saving measure and a scientific best practice — it ensures that your cohorts are comparable to those used in other OHDSI network studies, which is a prerequisite for meaningful cross-study synthesis.

title: Phenotyping
text:
5 Summary: the phenotyping workflow
1. ATLAS
   Build concept sets and cohort definitions
   ↓
2. CohortDiagnostics (R / HADES)
   Diagnose and validate phenotype behaviour across data sources
   ↓
3. PheValuator (R / HADES)       ←  if formal evaluation is needed
   Estimate sensitivity, specificity, PPV
   ↓
4. OHDSI Phenotype Library
   Search before building · Share after validating
A phenotype that has not been evaluated is a hypothesis, not a measurement. The tools above exist precisely to convert that hypothesis into a characterised, transparent, reproducible instrument — which is the standard expected in a GREG network study and, increasingly, in regulatory submissions to EMA and HTA bodies across Europe.

title: Diagnostics
text:
Running an analysis on a poorly specified cohort is worse than running no analysis at all! It can produce numbers that look credible but are wrong. Diagnostic tools exist to systematically surface problems with your phenotype algorithms and cohort logic before you commit to an analytical result.
In the OHDSI ecosystem, the diagnostic workflow centres on two tools: CohortDiagnostics and PhenotypeR. We will introduce PhenotypeR in this tutorial.

title: Diagnostics
text:
Running an analysis on a poorly specified cohort is worse than running no analysis at all — it produces numbers that look credible but are wrong. Diagnostic tools exist to systematically surface problems with your phenotype algorithms and cohort logic before you commit to an analytical result.
In the OHDSI/DARWIN EU ecosystem, the diagnostic workflow centres on two tools: CohortDiagnostics for population-level phenotype evaluation, and CohortCharacteristics for detailed baseline description. Think of these as your study’s quality control layer.

title: Diagnostics
text:
3 Setup
In this example, we better work with the Eunomia dataset as an example instead of the omock data, because the number and variety of drug exposures available in the synthetic data are more broad in the Eunomia dataset. You can also download example datasets from the omock package, like the GiBleed dataset. The documentation of the package is here.


Code
library(CohortConstructor)
library(CodelistGenerator)
library(CDMConnector)
library(omopgenerics)
library(omock)
library(dplyr)
library(duckdb)


requireEunomia()
db <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = eunomiaDir())
cdm <- cdmFromCon(db, 
                  cdmSchema = "main", 
                  writeSchema = "main", 
                  writePrefix = "greg_")


semaglutide <- getDrugIngredientCodes(cdm = cdm,
                                      name = "semaglutide")

t2dm <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition",
  includeDescendants = TRUE, 
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("type 2 diabetis mellitus", "T2DM")
)

acute_pancreatitis <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition", 
  includeDescendants = FALSE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("Acute pancreatitis")
)

# Build drug exposure cohorts (one per GLP-1 agent)
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = semaglutide,
  name        = "semaglutide_cohort",   # name of the cohort table in the CDM
  exit = "event_end_date",
  overlap = "merge")


# Build condition cohorts
cdm$t2dm_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = t2dm,
  name        = "t2dm_cohort"
)

cdm$ap_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = acute_pancreatitis,
  name        = "ap_cohort"
)

cdm <- bind(cdm$semaglutide_cohort, cdm$t2dm_cohort, cdm$ap_cohort, name = "study_cohorts")

title: Diagnostics
text:
3 1. Cohort counts and attrition
The first diagnostic is always: how many patients are in the cohort, and how many were lost at each step?


Code
# Cohort entry counts
count_result <- summariseCohortCount(cdm$glp1_cohorts)
tableCohortCount(count_result)

# Attrition (if you built the cohort with CohortConstructor)
attrition_result <- summariseCohortAttrition(cdm$glp1_cohorts)
tableCohortAttrition(attrition_result)

# Plot the attrition flowchart for one cohort
attrition_result |>
  filter(group_level == "semaglutide") |>
  plotCohortAttrition()



Our study: Review the attrition for each of the five GLP-1 RA cohorts side by side. Pay particular attention to whether the washout step removes a disproportionate fraction of patients in older agents (exenatide, liraglutide) compared to newer ones (tirzepatide). If so, this is expected — older drugs have more prevalent users by definition.

title: Diagnostics
text:
4 2. Index event breakdown
The index event breakdown tells you which specific concepts are driving cohort entry. For a drug cohort, this shows which branded products or formulations account for the most index dates.


Code
# Summarise the concept codes that appear on the index date
# (requires CohortDiagnostics — shown here conceptually)

# In CohortCharacteristics, use large scale characteristics
# restricted to the index date window
index_result <- cdm$glp1_cohorts |>
  summariseLargeScaleCharacteristics(
    window            = list(c(0, 0)),       # on index date only
    eventInWindow     = "drug_exposure",
    minimumFrequency  = 0.005                # only show if >0.5% of cohort
  )

tableTopLargeScaleCharacteristics(index_result)








NoteWhat to look for



For the semaglutide exposure cohort, you expect to see Ozempic (injectable) and Rybelsus (oral) as the dominant index concepts. If you see unexpected concepts — for example, a weight-loss branded product like Wegovy being excluded when you wanted to include it — your concept set needs revision.

title: Diagnostics
text:
5 3. Time distributions
How long do patients have prior observation before the index date? And how long do they remain in the cohort post-index?


Code
# Summarise cohort entry timing
timing_result <- summariseCohortTiming(cdm$glp1_cohorts)
tableCohortTiming(timing_result)

plotCohortTiming(
  timing_result,
  uniqueCombinations = TRUE,
  timeScale          = "years"
)



Our study: The distribution of prior observation time should show a minimum of 365 days (our washout + observation requirement). If you see patients with fewer than 365 days, your requireObservationBeforeDrug() criterion was not applied correctly. The distribution of post-index time tells you how much follow-up you have — if most patients have less than 6 months of follow-up, your 3-year HR estimate will be very imprecise.

title: Diagnostics
text:
6 4. Baseline characteristics
The core diagnostic for confounding: are the five GLP-1 RA cohorts comparable at baseline, or do they differ systematically in ways that could explain any observed difference in pancreatitis risk?


Code
# Summarise age, sex, and prior conditions
char_result <- summariseCharacteristics(
  cohort   = cdm$glp1_cohorts,
  ageGroup = list(c(18, 44), c(45, 64), c(65, 150)),
  tableIntersectCount = list(
    list(
      tableName  = "condition_occurrence",
      window     = c(-365, -1)
    )
  )
)

tableCharacteristics(char_result)

# Age distribution by cohort
char_result |>
  filter(variable_name == "Age") |>
  plotCharacteristics(
    plotType = "boxplot",
    colour   = "cohort_name"
  )

title: Diagnostics
text:
7 5. Large-scale characteristics — the SMD plot
The standardised mean difference (SMD) is the standard metric for assessing covariate balance across cohorts. An SMD below 0.1 for a covariate is generally considered indicative of no meaningful imbalance.


Code
# Large scale characteristics: all conditions, drugs, procedures
lsc_result <- cdm$glp1_cohorts |>
  summariseLargeScaleCharacteristics(
    window            = list(c(-365, -1)),    # 1 year prior to index
    eventInWindow     = c("condition_occurrence", "drug_exposure"),
    minimumFrequency  = 0.01                  # at least 1% prevalence
  )

# Comparison plot — SMD between cohorts
lsc_result |>
  plotComparedLargeScaleCharacteristics(
    reference = "semaglutide",
    colour    = "variable_level"
  )



Our study: After running large-scale characteristics across all five GLP-1 RA cohorts, we expect some imbalances. Key ones to look for:

Hypertriglyceridaemia — if more prevalent in older-drug cohorts (exenatide, liraglutide), this is a confounder for the pancreatitis outcome
Obesity — tirzepatide may be preferentially prescribed to more obese patients, which itself increases pancreatitis risk
Prior pancreatitis — must be inspected carefully; any prior acute pancreatitis should be handled as an exclusion criterion or sensitivity analysis


Quick check: You plot the SMD for 500 baseline covariates and find that hypertriglyceridaemia has an SMD of 0.32 between semaglutide and exenatide users. What does this tell you?
The difference is small and can be ignoredThere is meaningful imbalance — hypertriglyceridaemia should be included in the propensity score model as it is both a confounder and a risk factor for the outcomeYou should exclude all patients with hypertriglyceridaemiaThe cohort definitions are wrong and need to be redefined


Explanation

An SMD of 0.32 is well above the conventional threshold of 0.1, meaning hypertriglyceridaemia is meaningfully more prevalent in one exposure group than the other. Since hypertriglyceridaemia is also an independent risk factor for acute pancreatitis, it meets the definition of a confounder — it is associated with both treatment assignment and the outcome. It must be included in the propensity score model or adjusted for in the outcome model. Excluding patients with hypertriglyceridaemia would change your target population and invalidate the generalisability of your results.

title: Diagnostics
text:
8 6. Cohort overlap
Do patients appear in more than one of our five exposure cohorts? This should be rare or impossible if your new-user + washout criteria are correctly specified — a patient should only initiate one GLP-1 RA first.


Code
overlap_result <- summariseCohortOverlap(cdm$glp1_cohorts)
tableCohortOverlap(overlap_result)
plotCohortOverlap(overlap_result, uniqueCombinations = TRUE)








TipIf overlap is high



High overlap between exposure cohorts means your cohort exit criteria are not correctly excluding patients who switch between agents. For example, if a patient switches from liraglutide to semaglutide, they should exit the liraglutide cohort at the switch date and — if their second entry passes the washout criterion — enter the semaglutide cohort. Failure to handle this correctly leads to immortal time and misclassification bias.

title: Diagnostics
text:
9 Exporting diagnostics results


Code
# Combine all diagnostic results
all_diagnostics <- omopgenerics::bind(
  count_result,
  attrition_result,
  char_result,
  lsc_result,
  overlap_result
) |>
  omopgenerics::suppress(minCellCount = 5)  # privacy protection

# Export for sharing with study team
write.csv(all_diagnostics, "results/diagnostics.csv", row.names = FALSE)

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
Before running any code, it is worth being precise about what these two measures actually mean, because they answer to different questions.
Prevalence answers: what proportion of the population has this condition at a given point in time (or during a given period)? It captures both old and new cases.
Incidence answers: at what rate are new cases occurring in the at-risk population? It captures only new events in people who did not previously have the condition.








Measure
Formula
Answers




Point prevalence
Cases at time t / Population at time t
How common is this condition right now?


Period prevalence
Cases during period / Population during period
How common was it over this period?


Incidence proportion
New cases / At-risk persons
What is the risk of developing it?


Incidence rate
New cases / Person-time at risk
At what rate does it occur?



Sometimes we do not have the population at risk and our denominator changes to the overall population. Let’s think of the following example, in which we have a population with an underlying disease (population 1), a target population eligible to receive treatment (population 2) and an actually treated population (population 3). Incidence and prevalence would be as follows:

Figure. Incidence calculation in our example.








Note



Incidence rates are the most relevant measure for safety signal quantification and for risk-benefit assessments, they can be directly compared across populations and time periods. Prevalence is more relevant for burden-of-disease and healthcare resource utilisation analyses.


In this chapter we will work with the IncidencePrevalence package. The workflow always has three steps:
1. Generate the DENOMINATOR cohort (who is at risk and when?)
        ↓
2. Generate the OUTCOME cohort (who had the event?)
        ↓
3. Estimate incidence / prevalence using these two cohorts

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
2 The IncidencePrevalence package
The IncidencePrevalence package implements a principled, auditable workflow for computing these measures using OMOP CDM data. It was developed by the DARWIN EU Coordination Centre and is the standard tool for incidence/prevalence analyses across the OHDSI network.
The workflow always has three steps:
1. Generate the DENOMINATOR cohort (who is at risk and when?)
        ↓
2. Generate the OUTCOME cohort (who had the event?)
        ↓
3. Estimate incidence / prevalence using these two cohorts

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
2 Setup


Code
library(IncidencePrevalence)
library(CohortConstructor)
library(CodelistGenerator)
library(CDMConnector)
library(omopgenerics)
library(omock)
library(dplyr)
library(duckdb)


requireEunomia()
db <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = eunomiaDir())
cdm <- cdmFromCon(db, 
                  cdmSchema = "main", 
                  writeSchema = "main", 
                  writePrefix = "greg_")


semaglutide <- getDrugIngredientCodes(cdm = cdm,
                                      name = "semaglutide")

t2dm <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition",
  includeDescendants = TRUE, 
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("type 2 diabetis mellitus", "T2DM")
)

acute_pancreatitis <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition", 
  includeDescendants = FALSE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("Acute pancreatitis")
)

# Build drug exposure cohorts (one per GLP-1 agent)
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = semaglutide,
  name        = "semaglutide_cohort",   # name of the cohort table in the CDM
  exit = "event_end_date",
  overlap = "merge")


# Build condition cohorts
cdm$t2dm_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = t2dm,
  name        = "t2dm_cohort"
)

cdm$ap_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = acute_pancreatitis,
  name        = "ap_cohort"
)
cdm <- bind(cdm$semaglutide_cohort, cdm$t2dm_cohort, cdm$ap_cohort, name = "study_cohorts")

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
4 Step 1: Define the denominator population
The denominator defines who is at risk and for how long. You can restrict by age, sex, and a calendar study period.


Code
cdm <- generateDenominatorCohortSet(
  cdm                    = cdm,
  name                   = "denominator",
  cohortDateRange        = as.Date(c("2017-01-01", "2020-12-31")),
  ageGroup               = list(c(18, 44), c(45, 64), c(65, 150)),
  sex                    = c("Male", "Female", "Both"),
  daysPriorObservation   = 365   # require 1 year washout
)

# How many denominator cohorts were created?
cohortCount(cdm$denominator)


# A tibble: 9 × 3
  cohort_definition_id number_records number_subjects
                 <int>          <int>           <int>
1                    1           6185            6185
2                    2           6267            6267
3                    3          12452           12452
4                    4           5218            5218
5                    5           5318            5318
6                    6          10536           10536
7                    7           8460            8460
8                    8           8425            8425
9                    9          16885           16885



Our study: The denominator for the acute pancreatitis incidence analysis is the type 2 diabetes population. We define it as all T2DM patients with at least 365 days of prior observation, observed between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2025, stratified by age group (18–44, 45–64, 65+) and sex.

Quick check: Why do we require 365 days of prior observation in the denominator?
To ensure patients have had time to develop the outcomeTo exclude patients who may have had the outcome before the study period (washout), ensuring we only capture truly new (incident) casesBecause the IncidencePrevalence package requires itTo match the follow-up period of 365 days


Explanation

The washout period (daysPriorObservation) ensures that patients entering the denominator did not already have the outcome before their observation window began. Without it, we would count as “incident” cases patients who actually had a pre-existing condition — inflating the incidence rate. This is especially important for acute pancreatitis, where a patient admitted to hospital before the study period should not be counted as a new case.

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
5 Step 2: Define the outcome cohort
The outcome cohort identifies who experienced the event. For incidence, we need the first event per person during the at-risk period.


Code
# The mockIncidencePrevalence function pre-generates an outcome cohort
# In a real study, you would create it from conceptCohort() or ATLAS

# Check the outcome cohort exists
cdm$outcome |> cohortCount()


# A tibble: 1 × 3
  cohort_definition_id number_records number_subjects
                 <int>          <int>           <int>
1                    1           2500            2500


In a real study, you would build the acute pancreatitis outcome cohort:


Code
library(CohortConstructor)

# Acute pancreatitis — inpatient / emergency only (higher specificity)
cdm <- CohortConstructor::conceptCohort(
  cdm        = cdm,
  conceptSet = list(acute_pancreatitis = c(197456)),
  name       = "ap_outcome",
  domain     = "condition"
) 

# Restrict to inpatient / emergency care settings
cdm$ap_outcome <- cdm$ap_outcome |>
  CohortConstructor::requireTableIntersect(
    tableName    = "visit_occurrence",
    window       = c(0, 0),
    indexDate    = "cohort_start_date",
    # visit_concept_id 9201 = inpatient, 9203 = emergency
    conceptSet   = list(inpatient_emergency = c(9201, 9203)),
    name         = "ap_outcome"
  )

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
6 Step 3: Estimate incidence rates


Code
inc <- estimateIncidence(
  cdm             = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator",
  outcomeTable     = "outcome",
  interval         = "years",          # estimate per calendar year
  outcomeWashout   = 365,              # exclude patients with prior outcome
  repeatedEvents   = FALSE             # first event only per person
)

# # View results
# incidenceAttrition(inc)




Code
plotIncidence(inc,
  facet  = c("denominator_age_group"),
  colour = "denominator_sex"
)










Our study: Expected crude incidence of acute pancreatitis in a T2DM population is approximately 2–5 per 1,000 person-years. If your estimated rate is an order of magnitude higher, this indicates outcome misclassification — most likely because your outcome concept set is too broad and is capturing chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits or history codes. If it is zero or near-zero, check that your outcome concept IDs are correctly mapped in the OMOP vocabulary of your specific database.

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
7 Step 4: Estimate prevalence


Code
prev <- estimatePeriodPrevalence(
  cdm              = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator",
  outcomeTable     = "outcome",
  interval         = "years",
  fullContribution = FALSE   # patients contribute partial periods at edges
)

plotPrevalence(prev,
  facet  = "denominator_age_group",
  colour = "denominator_sex"
)















TipPoint prevalence vs period prevalence



Use estimatePointPrevalence() when you want a snapshot on a specific date (e.g. 1 January each year — useful for burden-of-disease estimates). Use estimatePeriodPrevalence() when you want to capture anyone with the condition during a time window (e.g. any quarter — useful for healthcare utilisation studies).

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
8 Stratification and subgroup analyses


Code
# Stratify by year and age group simultaneously
inc_stratified <- estimateIncidence(
  cdm              = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator",
  outcomeTable     = "outcome",
  interval         = "years",
  outcomeWashout   = 365
)

# Table output for sharing
tableIncidenceRates(inc_stratified, type = "flextable")

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
9 Suppression and export


Code
# Suppress small cell counts before sharing
results <- omopgenerics::bind(inc, prev) |>
  omopgenerics::suppress(minCellCount = 5)

write.csv(results, "results/incidence_prevalence.csv", row.names = FALSE)


Quick check: Your incidence rate estimate for acute pancreatitis is 45 per 1,000 person-years in the T2DM population. The published literature reports 2–5 per 1,000. What should you do first?
Accept the result — your database may have a sicker populationRestrict the age group to 65+ where pancreatitis is more commonInvestigate the outcome concept set — the high rate suggests you are likely capturing chronic pancreatitis, history codes, or outpatient follow-up visits as incident eventsIncrease the washout period to 5 years


Explanation

An incidence rate 10–20× higher than published estimates is almost always a signal of outcome phenotype misclassification. The most common cause in OMOP databases is that the concept set captures too many non-incident events — for example, SNOMED descendants that include chronic pancreatitis, billing codes used for follow-up visits after a previously diagnosed episode, or codes used as rule-outs rather than confirmed diagnoses. The correct response is to review your concept set in Athena, restrict to inpatient/emergency settings (which dramatically improves specificity for acute conditions), and potentially run CohortDiagnostics to inspect the index event breakdown.

title: Characterisation
text:
A characterisation study describes who is in a cohort, it is a descriptive study. It includes cohort demographics, comorbidities, medications, procedures, and healthcare utilisation at and around the index date. It does not make any causal claims. It answers the question: what does this population look like?

Disease natural history: to describe the clinical profile of patients with a condition over time
Treatment utilisation: to describe who receives a drug, under what circumstances, and with what co-treatments
Baseline comparability: to compare cohorts prior to a causal analysis to assess confounding and guide propensity score specification

Quick check: You are characterising the five GLP-1 RA cohorts. You find that 28% of exenatide users have a prior record of cholelithiasis, compared to 11% of semaglutide users. What is the SMD approximately, and what should you do?
SMD ≈ 0.17 — borderline, can be ignored if the outcome is not hepatobiliarySMD ≈ 0.17 — adjust in the outcome model onlySMD ≈ 0.47 — large imbalance; include cholelithiasis in the propensity score model since it is a strong confounder for APSMD ≈ 0.47 — exclude all patients with cholelithiasis from both cohorts


Explanation

The SMD for a binary variable is approximately (p1 - p2) / sqrt((p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)) / 2). Here: (0.28 - 0.11) / sqrt((0.28×0.72 + 0.11×0.89)/2) ≈ 0.17 / 0.36 ≈ 0.47. This is a large imbalance. Since cholelithiasis (gallstones) is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide, this is a strong confounder — it is both differentially distributed between the cohorts and directly causes the outcome. It must be included in the propensity score model. Excluding patients with cholelithiasis would change the target population and invalidate generalisation of the results.

title: Drug Utilisation
text:
A drug utilisation study (DUS) describes how a drug is used in clinical practice: who receives it, at what dose, for how long, for what indications, and in what combinations.
DUS are not causal analyses. They do not estimate the effect of a drug on an outcome. Their purpose is to describe, or characterise, real-world prescribing patterns. They are a key regulatory tool, regularly commissioned as post-authorisation safety studies (PASS) to monitor whether a drug is being used as intended.
Key questions a DUS answers:

Who is initiating the drug (demographics, comorbidities)?
What are the treatment patterns (dose, duration, adherence, switching)?
What are the indications for use?
Is the drug being used off-label?
What are co-prescriptions and concomitant medications?

3 Step 1: Create a drug cohort
The DrugUtilisation package provides generateIngredientCohortSet() as its primary cohort creation function. It creates drug era cohorts, collapsing consecutive prescription records with gaps below a specified threshold.


Code
# Create a cohort of acetaminophen users
# (proxy for our GLP-1 RA cohort in the real study)
cdm <- generateIngredientCohortSet(
  cdm        = cdm,
  name       = "dus_cohort",
  ingredient = "acetaminophen",
  gapEra     = 30    # collapse records with <30-day gaps into one era
)

# Restrict to first episode (new-user design)
cdm$dus_cohort <- cdm$dus_cohort |>
  requireIsFirstDrugEntry() |>
  requireObservationBeforeDrug(days = 365)

cohortCount(cdm$dus_cohort)

1                    1            168             168



Our study — creating GLP-1 RA drug cohorts: In the real analysis, we use a gap era of 30 days for once-weekly agents (semaglutide, dulaglutide, tirzepatide) and 7 days for twice-daily agents (exenatide immediate release). This reflects the expected prescription patterns and avoids artificially splitting continuous treatment episodes due to minor dispensing gaps.

Quick check: What does gapEra = 30 mean in generateIngredientCohortSet()?
Patients must have 30 days of observation before the drug startDrug exposure records with fewer than 30 days between the end of one record and the start of the next are collapsed into a single continuous eraThe drug cohort is restricted to the first 30 days of treatmentOnly prescriptions lasting at least 30 days are included


Explanation

gapEra controls the era collapsing logic. In claims or dispensing data, a patient on a once-weekly drug might have their 4-week prescription record end on day 28 and the next refill start on day 30 — a 2-day gap. Without era collapsing, these would appear as two separate drug eras (treatment discontinuation + restart). With gapEra = 30, gaps of fewer than 30 days are bridged, producing one continuous treatment era. The appropriate gap depends on the drug’s dosing frequency and the data source’s dispensing patterns.

Quick check: Your DUS shows that 35% of semaglutide users have no coded T2DM or obesity diagnosis in the 30 days before initiation. Does this mean 35% are receiving the drug off-label?
TRUEFALSE


Explanation

Not necessarily. In routine clinical databases, many patients with chronic conditions like T2DM do not have their diagnosis re-coded at every GP visit or prescription event. The absence of a recent coded diagnosis in the 30-day window does not mean the diagnosis is absent — it may simply not have been recorded recently. Looking at a wider window (e.g. any T2DM code ever in the patient’s history) typically reveals a much higher proportion with documented indication. The “no identifiable coded indication” category in a DUS is therefore best interpreted as a lower bound on true off-label use, not as the actual off-label rate.

title: Estimating effectiveness
text:
All the analyses in previous chapters were descriptive or exploratory. They are used to characterise populations, estimate rates, and describe drug utilisation. An effectiveness (or comparative safety) study attempts to estimate a causal effect of one treatment compared to another.






Note



The standard is to perform “comparative” studies (one treatment vs. another) instead of comparing to no treatment. This is to more closely reproduce a clinical trial framework and avoid selection bias.


Assessing causality is the hardest task in pharmacoepidemiology. Confounding is the central threat. In a randomised trial, random allocation ensures that confounders are distributed equally between groups. In observational data, we must adjust for confounding analytically, using tools like propensity scores, but we are restricted to the variables available in the data.
The preferred approach to causal inference from observational data is the new-user active-comparator cohort design with propensity score adjustment and negative control calibration.






Tip



In your protocol, you used the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework to define your research question and objectives. Keep that framework in mind during this chapter!

2 Setup
In this example, we better work with the Eunomia dataset as an example instead of the omock data, because the number and variety of drug exposures available in the synthetic data are more broad in the Eunomia dataset. You can also download example datasets from the omock package, like the GiBleed dataset. The documentation of the package is here.






Caution



In this setup section, we present a more realistic construction of cohorts introducing exitAtDeath() and relevant intersections with condition cohorts.




Code
library(CohortSurvival)
library(CohortMethod)
library(CohortConstructor)
library(CodelistGenerator)
library(CDMConnector)
library(omopgenerics)
library(omock)
library(dplyr)
library(duckdb)

requireEunomia()
db <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = eunomiaDir())
cdm <- cdmFromCon(db, 
                  cdmSchema = "main", 
                  writeSchema = "main", 
                  writePrefix = "greg_")


semaglutide <- getDrugIngredientCodes(cdm = cdm,
                                      name = "semaglutide")

tirzepatide <- getDrugIngredientCodes(cdm = cdm,
                                      name = "tirzepatide")

t2dm <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition",
  includeDescendants = TRUE, 
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("type 2 diabetis mellitus", "T2DM")
)

acute_pancreatitis <- getCandidateCodes(
  cdm = cdm,
  domains = "Condition", 
  includeDescendants = FALSE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE,
  keywords = c("Acute pancreatitis")
)

# Build exposure cohorts (one per GLP-1 agent)
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = semaglutide,
  name = "semaglutide_cohort",
  exit = "event_end_date",
  overlap = "merge"
)

cdm$tirzepatide_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = tirzepatide,
  name = "tirzepatide_cohort",
  exit = "event_end_date",
  overlap = "merge"
)

# Build the T2DM cohort
cdm$t2dm_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = t2dm,
  name = "t2dm_cohort"
)

# Keep only the first qualifying exposure record for each person.
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- requireIsFirstEntry(
  cdm$semaglutide_cohort,
  name = "semaglutide_cohort"
)

cdm$tirzepatide_cohort <- requireIsFirstEntry(
  cdm$tirzepatide_cohort,
  name = "tirzepatide_cohort"
)

# Keep only GLP-1 users who also have T2DM.
# Each exposure is intersected with T2DM separately.
cdm$semaglutide_t2dm <- requireCohortIntersect(
  cohort = cdm$semaglutide_cohort,
  targetCohortTable = "t2dm_cohort",
  window = list(c(-Inf, 0)),
  intersections = c(1, Inf),
  name = "semaglutide_t2dm"
)

cdm$tirzepatide_t2dm <- requireCohortIntersect(
  cohort = cdm$tirzepatide_cohort,
  targetCohortTable = "t2dm_cohort",
  window = list(c(-Inf, 0)),
  intersections = c(1, Inf),
  name = "tirzepatide_t2dm"
)

# Build the acute pancreatitis outcome cohort
cdm$ap_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = acute_pancreatitis,
  name = "ap_cohort"
)

# Exit at death; otherwise keep the existing cohort end date.
cdm$semaglutide_t2dm <- exitAtDeath(
  cdm$semaglutide_t2dm,
  name = "semaglutide_t2dm"
)

cdm$tirzepatide_t2dm <- exitAtDeath(
  cdm$tirzepatide_t2dm,
  name = "tirzepatide_t2dm"
)

# Combine the two exposure cohorts into one study target table.
cdm <- bind(
  cdm$semaglutide_t2dm,
  cdm$tirzepatide_t2dm,
  name = "study_cohorts"
)

6 Step 3: Propensity score estimation and matching

  connectionDetails      = connectionDetails,
  cdmDatabaseSchema      = "omop_cdm",

  riskWindowStart        = 0,
  riskWindowEnd          = 1095

  cohortMethodData = cohortMethodData,
  population       = studyPop

  scale         = "preference",

)








TipThe preference score plot is your most important diagnostic



Before matching, plot the propensity score distributions of the two cohorts on the preference score scale (which re-scales the PS to account for prevalence differences). If the distributions do not overlap substantially, matching is impossible for a large fraction of patients — you have an equipoise problem and your causal estimate will be extrapolating outside the region of common support.




Code

  population      = ps,
  caliper         = 0.2,           # 0.2 SD of log PS
  caliperScale    = "standardized logit",
  maxRatio        = 1              # 1:1 matching
)

# Check balance after matching
bal <- CohortMethod::computeCovariateBalance(matchedPop, cohortMethodData)
CohortMethod::plotCovariateBalanceScatterPlot(bal,
  showCovariateCountLabel = TRUE,
  showMaxLabel            = TRUE
)

title: GREGonBoard
text:
8 Step 5: Negative control calibration
This is the step that distinguishes a rigorous OHDSI analysis from a conventional pharmacoepidemiology study. Negative controls are outcomes where we know (from clinical reasoning) that the exposure has no causal effect. If our analysis pipeline has systematic error (residual confounding, outcome misclassification, time-at-risk misspecification), the negative control estimates will not be centred on a HR of 1.0.


Code
# Negative control outcomes (conditions causally unrelated to GLP-1 RAs)
# e.g. ingrown toenail, ankle sprain, foreign body in ear
negativeControlIds <- c(
  440448,  # ingrown nail
  81151,   # ankle sprain
  374914   # foreign body in ear
  # ... typically 50-100 negative controls
)

# Run the same analysis pipeline on all negative controls
ncResults <- CohortMethod::runCmAnalyses(
  connectionDetails = connectionDetails,
  # ... same settings as primary analysis
  # ... but with outcomeIds = negativeControlIds
)

# Fit calibration model
nullDist <- EmpiricalCalibration::fitMcmcNull(
  logRr   = ncResults$logRr,
  seLogRr = ncResults$seLogRr
)

# Plot the null distribution
EmpiricalCalibration::plotCalibrationEffect(
  logRrNegatives  = ncResults$logRr,
  seLogRrNegatives = ncResults$seLogRr,
  logRrPositives  = log(outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$estimate),
  seLogRrPositives = outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$logRrSe
)

# Apply calibration to the primary estimate
calibratedEstimate <- EmpiricalCalibration::calibrateP(
  null    = nullDist,
  logRr   = log(outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$estimate),
  seLogRr = outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$logRrSe
)
calibratedEstimate



Our study: If the negative control estimates are systematically shifted above HR = 1.0 (suggesting our analysis over-estimates risk), this means there is residual confounding — semaglutide users are sicker than liraglutide users in ways our propensity score did not fully capture. The calibrated HR corrects for this bias empirically. A calibrated p-value above the threshold after this correction means the primary finding is not robust to systematic error.

Quick check: After running 75 negative control outcomes through the same pipeline as your primary analysis, you find that the median HR for negative controls is 1.28 (rather than the expected 1.0). What does this tell you?
GLP-1 RAs increase risk of most conditions by 28%, which is a class effectYour negative control outcomes were not truly negative controlsThere is systematic positive bias in your analysis — likely residual confounding — which is inflating all HRs by approximately 28%; the calibration step will correct for thisThe propensity score model is perfectly calibrated


Explanation

A systematic shift in negative control estimates away from HR = 1.0 is the definition of systematic error in your analytical pipeline. Since negative controls are chosen specifically because GLP-1 RAs should have no causal effect on them, any deviation from 1.0 must be due to bias in the analysis — most commonly residual confounding (sicker patients in one group), differential observation (one group has more healthcare contacts and therefore more coded diagnoses), or immortal time bias. The EmpiricalCalibration package uses the distribution of negative control estimates to model this systematic error and correct the primary estimate and its p-value accordingly.

10 Interpreting the hazard ratio
Quick check: Your calibrated HR for acute pancreatitis comparing semaglutide vs. liraglutide is 0.87 (95% CI: 0.71–1.06, calibrated p = 0.18). What is the correct conclusion?
Semaglutide is significantly safer than liraglutide for pancreatitisLiraglutide is significantly safer than semaglutide for pancreatitisThere is no statistically significant difference in acute pancreatitis risk between semaglutide and liraglutide; the point estimate suggests a possible 13% lower risk with semaglutide but the confidence interval includes 1.0The study is underpowered and should be repeated with a larger sample


Explanation

A HR of 0.87 with a 95% CI of 0.71–1.06 means the confidence interval includes 1.0 (no difference). The calibrated p-value of 0.18 is above any conventional threshold for statistical significance. The correct conclusion is that we found no statistically significant difference in acute pancreatitis risk between the two agents. The point estimate is directionally consistent with a small advantage for semaglutide, but the evidence is insufficient to conclude a true difference exists. This is a clinically important null finding — it provides reassurance that both agents carry similar pancreatitis risk in real-world T2DM populations.

title: Codelist Generator
text:
A concept set is the fundamental vocabulary unit of any OMOP study. At its most basic, it is a named collection of standard concept IDs grouped together because they collectively represent a single clinical idea relevant to your research question. A concept set is not a list of ICD-10 codes, SNOMED terms, or RxNorm strings: it is a list of OMOP standard concept IDs, which are the normalised, source-agnostic representations that the ETL process maps all original source codes into.






Important



This distinction is critical! If your study site records a diagnosis using ICD-10 code E11.9 (Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications), and another site uses the Read code C10F, both are (or should be) mapped during the ETL to the same OMOP standard concept ID for type 2 diabetes mellitus (SNOMED 201826). A concept set defined using that standard ID will therefore capture patients from both sites identically, regardless of the original coding system used!


In practice, a concept set rarely consists of a single concept ID, not even multiple concept IDs from the same domain, like we saw in the Phenotyping and ATLAS sections. A concept set that is too broad will capture false-positive patients; one that is too narrow will miss true cases. Both forms of misclassification bias the results in different directions depending on the study design.
You can build concept sets with the CodelistGenerator package or with ATLAS.

In our example study:
Objectives (as in Study Protocol)


Calculate the yearly prevalence and incidence proportion and density of GLP-1 receptor agonists given as a treatment to type 2 diabetes patients.
Characterise the users of each GLP-1 receptor agonists, including sociodemographic, clinical and large-scale characteristics.
Define the mean duration of treatment and treatment patterns, including switches, for patients with type 2 diabetes exposed to GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Assess the comparative safety of the different GLP-1 receptor agonists against acute pancreatitis outcomes.


We need several concept sets: one concept set per each of the five GLP-1 receptor agonist agents of interest at the ingredient level with descendants, to ensure every branded formulation and dose strength is included. The type 2 diabetes mellitus concept set, in which we must include the T2DM concept and its descendants, but explicitly excluding any concepts that overlap with type 1 diabetes or secondary diabetes, to avoid misclassifying the population. And finally, the acute pancreatitis concept set, which must balance sensitivity (capturing all truly incident cases) against specificity (excluding chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits and historical coding).

title: Codelist Generator
text:
A cohort is the fundamental unit of analysis in OMOP observational research. Formally, a cohort is a set of persons who satisfy one or more inclusion criteria for a duration of time. In OMOP, every cohort is stored as a table with exactly four columns:







Column
Description




cohort_definition_id
Integer identifying which cohort definition this row belongs to


subject_id
The person_id of the patient


cohort_start_date
The date the patient enters the cohort (Day 0 / index date)


cohort_end_date
The date the patient exits the cohort



This simple structure is powerful: one patient can appear multiple times (e.g. multiple treatment episodes), and one table can hold many different cohort definitions simultaneously.






NoteTwo ways to build cohorts



ATLAS: graphical interface, produces CIRCE-BE JSON → SQL. Best for sharing definitions across a network via JSON export.
CohortConstructor (R): programmatic pipeline using dplyr-style syntax. Best for complex multi-step cohort logic, sensitivity analyses, and automated pipelines.
Both produce the same four-column cohort table. They are complementary, not competing.

3 Building a cohort from concept sets
The most common starting point is conceptCohort(): define a cohort by the presence of a concept (or concept set) in a given domain table.


Code
# Define concept sets as named lists of concept IDs
glp1_concepts <- list(
  semaglutide  = c(2200644),   # RxNorm ingredient
  liraglutide  = c(1474828),
  dulaglutide  = c(1551099),
  exenatide    = c(1544838),
  tirzepatide  = c(37003518)
)

  type2_diabetes = c(201826)   # SNOMED concept + descendants via ATLAS
)

  acute_pancreatitis = c(197456)  # SNOMED

  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = glp1_concepts,
  name        = "glp1_cohorts",   # name of the cohort table in the CDM
  domain      = "drug"            # look in drug_exposure
)

# Build condition cohorts

  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = t2dm_concepts,
  name        = "t2dm_cohort",
  domain      = "condition"
)

cdm <- CohortConstructor::conceptCohort(

2 Evaluating a phenotype
When we evaluate a phenotype algorithm, we are essentially asking: of all the patients in the database who truly have the condition, how many does our algorithm correctly identify (sensitivity)? And of all the patients our algorithm flags, how many truly have the condition (positive predictive value / specificity)?






Note



Sensitivity measures how well a test correctly identifies people who have a condition, while specificity measures how well a test correctly identifies people who do not have it.


These two properties pull in opposite directions, and the right trade-off depends on the study type:








Study type
Priority
Rationale




Incidence / prevalence
High sensitivity
Better to capture all cases, even if some are false positives


Safety outcome (rare event)
High specificity
A false positive outcome event can create a spurious safety signal


Exposure definition
High specificity
Misclassifying non-users as users is a major source of confounding


Characterisation
Balanced
Describes the cohort as captured; misclassification affects interpretation




Let’s go back to our study example. Why does specificity matter more for the outcome? Acute pancreatitis is a serious adverse event with a relatively low background incidence (~2-5 per 1,000 person-years in T2DM patients). A low-specificity outcome phenotype, that is, a phenotype that captures chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits, pancreatitis history codes, or rule-out diagnoses coded as confirmatory, would inflate the event count and potentially dilute or distort the hazard ratio. For this reason, restricting the outcome to inpatient or emergency settings is a deliberate specificity-improving decision, even at the cost of some sensitivity.

Quick check: You are designing the outcome phenotype for acute pancreatitis. You have two options: (A) any condition occurrence record for acute pancreatitis in any care setting, or (B) at least one inpatient or emergency acute pancreatitis record. Which has higher specificity?
Option AOption BThey have the same specificityIt depends on the database


Explanation

Option B has higher specificity because restricting to inpatient or emergency settings filters out the codes most likely to represent historical diagnoses, follow-up visits for previously diagnosed pancreatitis, or diagnostic uncertainty (where a clinician codes a rule-out condition). Nevertheless, outpatient acute pancreatitis codes are far more likely to be false positives than inpatient codes, where the diagnosis typically requires clinical examination, laboratory findings, and often imaging confirmation. The trade-off is reduced sensitivity: some true acute pancreatitis events managed in outpatient settings will be missed; but for a rare serious adverse event, this trade-off is generally acceptable.

section: 3 Tools for phenotyping and evaluating phenotypes
text:
3 Tools for phenotyping and evaluating phenotypes
The OHDSI ecosystem provides a structured, layered set of tools that cover the full phenotyping workflow: from building concept sets and cohort definitions, to diagnosing their performance, to formally evaluating their sensitivity and specificity, to sharing validated definitions with the global community.

3.1 The OHDSI Phenotype Library
The OHDSI Phenotype Library is the community’s shared repository of cohort definitions, subject to version control, open peer review, and regular quality checks across the OHDSI network. Each entry includes not only the cohort definition JSON (from ATLAS) but also clinical descriptions, evaluation results from CohortDiagnostics and PheValuator, contributor attribution, and a stable DOI that can be cited in publications.


3.2 Building the phenotype: ATLAS/CodelistGenerator+CohortConstructor
ATLAS is a web tool where you can build your concept sets and cohort definitions. The cohort definition is the phenotype algorithm in its executable form (a JSON specification that can be run against any OMOP CDM database). If you are using R instead of ATLAS, you can use the packages CodelistGenerator and CohortConstructor, which will be explained in the following sections. The executable form is then the R script itself since you create the cohorts in your OMOP CDM database, and you do not need the JSON file.
The key decisions at this stage are:

Which concept(s) to use and whether to include descendants
Which OMOP domain(s) to search (condition occurrence, drug exposure, measurement, etc.)
What temporal logic to apply (first ever occurrence, any occurrence, occurrence within a window)
What additional inclusion and exclusion criteria to apply







Tip



Before designing a phenotype from scratch, always search the OHDSI Phenotype Library! It is a publicly accessible, version-controlled catalogue of peer-reviewed cohort definitions contributed by the OHDSI community. Each entry includes clinical descriptions, technical logic, evaluation results, and a stable DOI.


This section is further developed in the ATLAS, CodelistGenerator and CohortConstructor chapters.


3.3 Diagnosing the phenotype: CohortDiagnostics/PhenotypeR
CohortDiagnostics and PhenotypeR are R packages that produce a standardised battery of diagnostics for any cohort definition, without sharing patient-level data. It is the essential next step after building a cohort and before running any analysis. They help ascertain whether you have created your cohort properly or you might be missing something (or someone).
This section is further developed in the Diagnostics chapter.


3.4 Evaluating sensitivity and specificity with PheValuator
PheValuator is an R package that provides a semi-automated method for estimating the sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) of a phenotype algorithm without requiring manual chart review. It does this by building a diagnostic prediction model using a cohort of patients very likely to be true positives (the xSpec — extremely specific cohort — defined by requiring multiple diagnostic codes over time) and applying it to a large random sample of the database to generate a predicted probability of the condition for every patient. These probabilities are then used as a probabilistic gold standard against which the rule-based phenotype algorithm is evaluated.
The key outputs of PheValuator are:

Sensitivity: the proportion of true cases captured by the phenotype algorithm
Specificity: the proportion of true non-cases correctly excluded
PPV: the proportion of algorithm-identified cases that are true cases
NPV: the proportion of algorithm-excluded patients that are true non-cases







Note



This is a nice addition to the phenotyping process, but it is not a required step.

title: Codelist Generator
text:
A concept set is the fundamental vocabulary unit of any OMOP study. At its most basic, it is a named collection of standard concept IDs grouped together because they collectively represent a single clinical idea relevant to your research question. A concept set is not a list of ICD-10 codes, SNOMED terms, or RxNorm strings: it is a list of OMOP standard concept IDs, which are the normalised, source-agnostic representations that the ETL process maps all original source codes into.






Important



This distinction is critical! If your study site records a diagnosis using ICD-10 code E11.9 (Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications), and another site uses the Read code C10F, both are (or should be) mapped during the ETL to the same OMOP standard concept ID for type 2 diabetes mellitus (SNOMED 201826). A concept set defined using that standard ID will therefore capture patients from both sites identically, regardless of the original coding system used!


In practice, a concept set rarely consists of a single concept ID, not even multiple concept IDs from the same domain, like we saw in the Phenotyping and ATLAS sections. A concept set that is too broad will capture false-positive patients; one that is too narrow will miss true cases. Both forms of misclassification bias the results in different directions depending on the study design.
You can build concept sets with the CodelistGenerator package or with ATLAS.

In our example study:
Objectives (as in Study Protocol)


Calculate the yearly prevalence and incidence proportion and density of GLP-1 receptor agonists given as a treatment to type 2 diabetes patients.
Characterise the users of each GLP-1 receptor agonists, including sociodemographic, clinical and large-scale characteristics.
Define the mean duration of treatment and treatment patterns, including switches, for patients with type 2 diabetes exposed to GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Assess the comparative safety of the different GLP-1 receptor agonists against acute pancreatitis outcomes.


We need several concept sets: one concept set per each of the five GLP-1 receptor agonist agents of interest at the ingredient level with descendants, to ensure every branded formulation and dose strength is included. The type 2 diabetes mellitus concept set, in which we must include the T2DM concept and its descendants, but explicitly excluding any concepts that overlap with type 1 diabetes or secondary diabetes, to avoid misclassifying the population. And finally, the acute pancreatitis concept set, which must balance sensitivity (capturing all truly incident cases) against specificity (excluding chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits and historical coding).

 No, because we are defining conditions. It is not necessary, but we might make a more complete definition if we include other concepts like drug exposures or measurements that might be related to the conditions. Yes, we should always include all domains because that is the way to make the most complete definition of all concepts.

title: Incidence-Prevalence
text:
Before running any code, it is worth being precise about what these two measures actually mean, because they answer to different questions.
Prevalence answers: what proportion of the population has this condition at a given point in time (or during a given period)? It captures both old and new cases.
Incidence answers: at what rate are new cases occurring in the at-risk population? It captures only new events in people who did not previously have the condition.








Measure
Formula
Answers




Point prevalence
Cases at time t / Population at time t
How common is this condition right now?


Period prevalence
Cases during period / Population during period
How common was it over this period?


Incidence proportion
New cases / At-risk persons
What is the risk of developing it?


Incidence rate
New cases / Person-time at risk
At what rate does it occur?



Sometimes we do not have the population at risk and our denominator changes to the overall population. Let’s think of the following example, in which we have a population with an underlying disease (population 1), a target population eligible to receive treatment (population 2) and an actually treated population (population 3). Incidence and prevalence would be as follows:



Figure. Prevalence calculation in our example.





Figure. Incidence calculation in our example.








Note



Incidence rates are the most relevant measure for safety signal quantification and for risk-benefit assessments, they can be directly compared across populations and time periods. Prevalence is more relevant for burden-of-disease and healthcare resource utilisation analyses.


In this chapter we will work with the IncidencePrevalence package. The workflow always has three steps:
1. Generate the DENOMINATOR cohort (who is at risk and when?)
        ↓
2. Generate the OUTCOME cohort (who had the event?)
        ↓
3. Estimate incidence / prevalence using these two cohorts

In this tutorial we will provide an example on how to calculate incidence and prevalence with IncidencePrevalence, but further documentation can be found in the package documentation, with all available functions in its reference index and in this other tutorial.

3.1 Step 1: Define the denominator population
The denominator defines who is at risk and for how long. You can restrict by age, sex, and a calendar study period. An “overall population” denominator for our study would be, if we wanted to stratify incidence and prevalence by age group (18-44, 45-64, 65+) and sex.:


Code
cdm <- generateDenominatorCohortSet(
  cdm                    = cdm,
  name                   = "denominator",
  cohortDateRange        = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2025-12-31")),
  ageGroup               = list(c(18, 44), c(45, 64), c(65, 150)),
  sex                    = c("Male", "Female", "Both"),
  daysPriorObservation   = 365 # coherent with the numerator cohort
)








Note



In our study, the denominator for the acute pancreatitis incidence analysis would be the type 2 diabetes population taking a GLP-1 RA, if we consider “population at risk”.


Quick check: Why do we require 365 days of prior observation in the denominator?
To ensure patients have had time to develop the outcomeTo exclude patients who may have had the outcome before the study period (washout), ensuring we only capture truly new (incident) casesBecause the IncidencePrevalence package requires itTo match the follow-up period of 365 days


Explanation

The washout period (daysPriorObservation) ensures that patients entering the denominator did not already have the outcome before their observation window began. We want to discard them from the denominator because we could not include those patients in the numerator neither.



3.2 Step 2: Define the outcome cohort
The outcome cohort identifies who experienced the event. For incidence, we need the first event per person during the at-risk period. For prevalence, all events are valid.

In our example, this would be the ap_cohort we already created.



3.3 Step 3: Estimate incidence rates


Code
inc <- estimateIncidence(
  cdm             = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator", # or t2dm + each GLP1-RA
  outcomeTable     = "ap_cohort",
  interval         = "years",       # estimate per calendar year
  outcomeWashout   = 365,           # exclude patients with prior outcome
  repeatedEvents   = FALSE          # first event only per person
)








Note



Our study: The expected crude incidence of acute pancreatitis in a T2DM population is approximately 3-6 per 1,000 person-years1. If your estimated rate is an order of magnitude higher, something happened. The most probable reason is outcome misclassification, most likely because your outcome concept set is too broad and is capturing chronic pancreatitis follow-up visits or history codes. If it is zero or near-zero, check that your outcome concept IDs are correctly mapped in the OMOP vocabulary of your specific database.


Quick check: Your incidence rate estimate for acute pancreatitis is 45 per 1,000 person-years in the T2DM population. The published literature reports 3-6 per 1,000. What should you do first?
Accept the result, your database may have a sicker populationTalk to the data providers to see if they have an issue with the dataInvestigate the outcome concept set, you are likely capturing chronic pancreatitis, history codes, or outpatient follow-up visits as incident eventsCheck your code, maybe you are multiplying by 10 where you should not!


Explanation

An incidence rate 10-20× higher than published estimates is almost always a signal of outcome phenotype misclassification. The most common cause in OMOP databases is that the concept set captures too many non-incident events. For example, SNOMED descendants that include chronic pancreatitis, billing codes used for follow-up visits after a previously diagnosed episode, or codes used as rule-outs rather than confirmed diagnoses. The correct response is to review your concept set and restrict your events.







Tip



Do not hesitate to contact the data providers and even discuss results with them if they do not make sense! First, make sure that it is not a coding and/or phenotyping error, but if results do not make sense after careful revision of everything that could have gone wrong with your data analysis pipeline, perhaps something happens with the data that you are not considering! Not that it is wrong, or wrongly mapped. Perhaps using a system which you had not considered!




3.4 Step 4: Estimate prevalence


Code
prev <- estimatePeriodPrevalence(
  cdm              = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator", # or t2dm + each GLP1-RA
  outcomeTable     = "ap_cohort",
  interval         = "years",
  fullContribution = FALSE   # patients contribute partial periods at edges
)

pointPrev <- estimatePointPrevalence(
  cdm              = cdm,
  denominatorTable = "denominator", # or t2dm + each GLP1-RA
  outcomeTable     = "ap_cohort",
  interval         = "years"
)








Tip



Use estimatePointPrevalence() when you want a snapshot on a specific date (useful for burden-of-disease estimates). Use estimatePeriodPrevalence() when you want to capture anyone with the condition during a time window (useful for healthcare utilisation studies).



3.4.1 Stratification and subgroup analyses
To obtain results stratified by age or sex, you only need to include them in your cohort definitions. To include stratification by an additional group, you can add this variable to your functions: strata = list() listing the groups by which you want to stratify (and you should have defined them previously).
Quick check: The way we have written it in code, are we stratifying incidence and prevalence by age and sex? Yes, but only incidence.Yes, but only period prevalence.Yes because by design it is included.No, we would need to specify it.
