text:
3 Example pipeline
In this tutorial we will provide an example on how to build the cohorts for our study with CohortConstructor, but further documentation can be found in the package documentation, with all available functions in its reference index and in this other tutorial or this one.

3.1 1. Building a cohort from concept sets
The most common starting point is conceptCohort(): define a cohort by the presence of a concept (or concept set) in a given domain table. Remember that we have our concept sets already from the Codelist Generator section!


Code
library(CohortConstructor)
  
# Build drug exposure cohorts (one per GLP-1 agent)
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = semaglutide,
  name        = "semaglutide_cohort",   # name of the cohort table in the CDM
  exit = "event_end_date",
  overlap = "merge")


# Build condition cohorts
cdm$t2dm_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = t2dm,
  name        = "t2dm_cohort"
)

cdm$ap_cohort <- conceptCohort(
  cdm         = cdm,
  conceptSet  = acute_pancreatitis,
  name        = "ap_cohort"
)



Our study: We create five separate exposure cohorts, one per GLP-1 RA ingredient. The conceptCohort() function creates one cohort entry per drug exposure episode per patient. The next steps will apply the new-user and other inclusion criteria.



3.2 2. Applying inclusion criteria with require()
The new-user design requires that patients have no prior use of any GLP-1 RA before their index date. We implement this in two steps: first restricting to first entry per person, then requiring no prior exposure.


Code
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- cdm$semaglutide_cohort |>
  requireIsFirstEntry() |> # Keep only the first exposure episode per patient
  requireObservationBeforeDrug(
    days = 365    # at least 365 days prior observation
  ) |>
  requirePriorDrugWashout(
    days = 365 # Restrict to patients with no prior semaglutide in 365 days before index
  ) |>
  requireAge(
    ageRange = list(c(18, 150)) # Restrict to only adults 
  )
  requireInDateRange(
    dateRange = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2025-12-31")) # Restrict to the study period
  ) 








Important



You need to have the 365 days observation period prior to the index date if you want to be able to apply the washout period of 365 days for new use! If you do not have this previous period of observation you are not able to discern whether a previous use has happened in these days.




3.3 3. Requiring presence in another cohort
Patients must have a T2DM diagnosis on or before the index date:


Code
cdm$semaglutide_cohort <- cdm$semaglutide_cohort |>
  requireCohortIntersect(
    cohortTable      = "t2dm_cohort",
    cohortId         = 1,
    window           = c(-Inf, 0),   # any time before or on index date
    intersections    = c(1, Inf),    # at least 1 intersection required
    name             = "semaglutide_cohort"
  )








TipThe order matters!



The order in which you introduce the inclusion criteria will have an impact on your final cohort. When you plot the attrition of the cohort building process, you will see how your sample of patients becomes increasingly restricted by your inclusion criteria. You might decide to be more strict or loose in some criteria depending on that! Try to start by more general rules and become more precise in the end of the pipeline. Or try to implement your most important restriction criteria first.


Do you think that the order that we followed for the construction of the cohort of semaglutide is correct?
Yes, from general to specificYes, from unavoidable to changeableNo, you should do the most general criteria first, like date rangeYes, but I do not understand the order


Explanation

The order we applied here is from the most unavoidable to the least. We want to define a new-user cohort, therefore restricting to first entry and making sure that the first entry is well-captured is a must. If we would like incident entry and not first entry, we should just remove the requireIsFirstEntry() command but all other restrictions apply. Finally, we can more easily adapt the study period than change the age restriction for our study, because this could also be drug/condition dependant.



3.4 4. Finishing details
Here we created simple cohorts that exit at the end of an exposure or observation. We might want to specify other reasons for exit, such as entering another cohort, switching exposures, or even death. You can also do that and be sure to create properly your cohort definitions before continuing with the analyses.


3.5 5. Checking cohort counts and attrition
After building the cohort, we can inspect the attrition table, as it shows how many patients were excluded at each step, which is essential for transparency and for detecting logic errors. You can do that running diagnostics on your cohorts, as you will see in the Diagnostics section.






Tip



Always check your attrition table or plot! And make sure to run the appropriate diagnostics to your cohorts!




3.6 6. Exporting cohort definitions


Code
# Export cohort table to a local file for sharing or archiving
cohort_data <- cdm$semaglutide_cohort |> collect()
write.csv(cohort_data, "results/semaglutide_cohort.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Disconnect
dbDisconnect(con)

title: Estimating effectiveness
text:
All the analyses in previous chapters were descriptive or exploratory. They are used to characterise populations, estimate rates, and describe drug utilisation. An effectiveness (or comparative safety) study attempts to estimate a causal effect of one treatment compared to another.






Note



The standard is to perform “comparative” studies (one treatment vs. another) instead of comparing to no treatment. This is to more closely reproduce a clinical trial framework and avoid selection bias.


Assessing causality is the hardest task in pharmacoepidemiology. Confounding is the central threat. In a randomised trial, random allocation ensures that confounders are distributed equally between groups. In observational data, we must adjust for confounding analytically, using tools like propensity scores, but we are restricted to the variables available in the data.
The preferred approach to causal inference from observational data is the new-user active-comparator cohort design with propensity score adjustment and negative control calibration. This has been implemented in the CohortMethod R package.






Tip



In your protocol, you used the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework to define your research question and objectives. Keep that framework in mind during this chapter!

title: Estimating effectiveness
text:
1.2 Step 5: Negative control calibration
This is the step that distinguishes a rigorous OHDSI analysis from a conventional pharmacoepidemiology study. Negative controls are outcomes where we know (from clinical reasoning) that the exposure has no causal effect. If our analysis pipeline has systematic error (residual confounding, outcome misclassification, time-at-risk misspecification), the negative control estimates will not be centred on a HR of 1.0.


Code
# Negative control outcomes (conditions causally unrelated to GLP-1 RAs)

# e.g. ingrown toenail, ankle sprain, foreign body in ear

negativeControlIds <- c(

  440448,  # ingrown nail

  81151,   # ankle sprain

  374914   # foreign body in ear

  # ... typically 50-100 negative controls

)

# Run the same analysis pipeline on all negative controls

ncResults <- CohortMethod::runCmAnalyses(

  connectionDetails = connectionDetails,

  # ... same settings as primary analysis

  # ... but with outcomeIds = negativeControlIds

)

# Fit calibration model

nullDist <- EmpiricalCalibration::fitMcmcNull(

  logRr   = ncResults$logRr,

  seLogRr = ncResults$seLogRr

)

# Plot the null distribution

EmpiricalCalibration::plotCalibrationEffect(

  logRrNegatives  = ncResults$logRr,

  seLogRrNegatives = ncResults$seLogRr,

  logRrPositives  = log(outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$estimate),

  seLogRrPositives = outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$logRrSe

)

# Apply calibration to the primary estimate

calibratedEstimate <- EmpiricalCalibration::calibrateP(

  null    = nullDist,

  logRr   = log(outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$estimate),

  seLogRr = outcomeModel$outcomeModelTreatmentEstimate$logRrSe

)

calibratedEstimate



Our study: If the negative control estimates are systematically shifted above HR = 1.0 (suggesting our analysis over-estimates risk), this means there is residual confounding — semaglutide users are sicker than liraglutide users in ways our propensity score did not fully capture. The calibrated HR corrects for this bias empirically. A calibrated p-value above the threshold after this correction means the primary finding is not robust to systematic error.

Quick check: After running 75 negative control outcomes through the same pipeline as your primary analysis, you find that the median HR for negative controls is 1.28 (rather than the expected 1.0). What does this tell you?
GLP-1 RAs increase risk of most conditions by 28%, which is a class effectYour negative control outcomes were not truly negative controlsThere is systematic positive bias in your analysis — likely residual confounding — which is inflating all HRs by approximately 28%; the calibration step will correct for thisThe propensity score model is perfectly calibrated


Explanation

A systematic shift in negative control estimates away from HR = 1.0 is the definition of systematic error in your analytical pipeline. Since negative controls are chosen specifically because GLP-1 RAs should have no causal effect on them, any deviation from 1.0 must be due to bias in the analysis — most commonly residual confounding (sicker patients in one group), differential observation (one group has more healthcare contacts and therefore more coded diagnoses), or immortal time bias. The EmpiricalCalibration package uses the distribution of negative control estimates to model this systematic error and correct the primary estimate and its p-value accordingly.

1.4 Interpreting the hazard ratio
Quick check: Your calibrated HR for acute pancreatitis comparing semaglutide vs. liraglutide is 0.87 (95% CI: 0.71–1.06, calibrated p = 0.18). What is the correct conclusion?
Semaglutide is significantly safer than liraglutide for pancreatitisLiraglutide is significantly safer than semaglutide for pancreatitisThere is no statistically significant difference in acute pancreatitis risk between semaglutide and liraglutide; the point estimate suggests a possible 13% lower risk with semaglutide but the confidence interval includes 1.0The study is underpowered and should be repeated with a larger sample


Explanation

A HR of 0.87 with a 95% CI of 0.71–1.06 means the confidence interval includes 1.0 (no difference). The calibrated p-value of 0.18 is above any conventional threshold for statistical significance. The correct conclusion is that we found no statistically significant difference in acute pancreatitis risk between the two agents. The point estimate is directionally consistent with a small advantage for semaglutide, but the evidence is insufficient to conclude a true difference exists. This is a clinically important null finding — it provides reassurance that both agents carry similar pancreatitis risk in real-world T2DM populations.

text:
3 Example pipeline
In this tutorial we will provide an example on how to do a DUS with DrugUtilisation, but further documentation can be found in the package documentation, with all available functions in its reference index and in this other tutorial or this training.

3.1 Step 1: Create a drug cohort
The DrugUtilisation package provides generateIngredientCohortSet() as its primary cohort creation function. It creates drug cohorts, collapsing consecutive prescription records with gaps below a specified threshold.


Code
# Create semaglutide cohort as ingredient
cdm <- generateIngredientCohortSet(
  cdm        = cdm,
  name       = "semaglutide_dus_cohort",
  ingredient = "semaglutide",
  gapEra     = 365    # this number depends on how recurrent prescriptions for this ingredient's medications are
) 

cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort <- cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort|>
  requireIsFirstDrugEntry() |> # First entry, like before
  requireObservationBeforeDrug(days = 365) # Prior observation period, like before!



Our study: we have already done our cohorts for GLP-1 RA with the conceptCohort() function. There is no need to repeat that. These are two different options: the generateIngredientCohortSet() allows you to go for ingredient level, while the conceptCohort() allows you to use specific products and dose forms.

Quick check: What does gapEra = 365 mean in generateIngredientCohortSet()?
Patients must have 365 days of observation before the drug startDrug exposure records with fewer than 365 days between the end of one record and the start of the next are collapsed into a single continuous eraThe drug cohort is restricted to the first 365 days of treatmentOnly prescriptions lasting at least 365 days are included


Explanation

gapEra controls the era collapsing logic. In claims or dispensing data, a patient on a once-weekly drug might have their 4-week prescription record end on day 28 and the next refill start on day 30, a 2-day gap. Without era collapsing, these would appear as two separate drug eras (treatment discontinuation + restart). With gapEra = 365, gaps of fewer than 365 days are bridged, producing one continuous treatment era. The appropriate gap depends on the drug’s dosing frequency and the data source’s dispensing patterns.



3.2 Step 2: Treatment duration and exposure


Code
dus_result <- cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort |>
  summariseDrugUtilisation(
    ingredientConceptId = 793143,  # semaglutide
    gapEra              = 365,     # change at convenience
    estimates           = c("q25", "median", "q75", "mean", "sd")
  )

dus_result |>
  filter(variable_name %in% c(
    "days prescribed",
    "days exposed",
    "number eras",
    "initial daily dose milligram"
  )) |>
  select(variable_name, estimate_name, estimate_value)



Exercise!
For each GLP-1 RA agent, report:







Metric
Clinical interpretation




Days prescribed (median, IQR)

3.3 Step 3: Indications for use
What conditions were patients treated for? This is especially relevant for GLP-1 RAs, which are licensed for T2DM and obesity but increasingly used off-label.


Code
# Define indication cohorts
indications <- list(headache  = 378253, influenza = 4266367, t2dm = 201826)

cdm$indications_cohort <- conceptCohort(cdm = cdm,
                                        conceptSet = indications,
                                        name = "indications_cohort")

indication_result <- cdm$dus_cohort |>
  summariseIndication(
    indicationCohortName = "indications_cohort",
    unknownIndicationTable  = "condition_occurrence",
    indicationWindow        = list(c(-30, 0)) # You can select the most appropriate window for your analysis
  )

indication_result |>
  filter(estimate_name == "percentage") |>
  select(variable_level, estimate_value) 


Quick check: You run the summarise indication function for semaglutide and most of the indications are unknown. What is the most plausible cause?

Semaglutide is being used off-label more than what we thought: TRUEFALSE
Indication is not well-recorded in the database: TRUEFALSE
We have not created a good enough indications cohort: TRUEFALSE



3.4 Step 4: Treatment adherence
The DrugUtilisation package allows you to compute treatment adherence in two different ways: - Proportion of Days Covered (PDC): the standard measure of medication adherence in claims data. PDC ≥ 80% is the conventional threshold for “adherent.” - As a survival analysis using the CohortSurvival package. The function assumes that each cohort entry is a continuous treatment era.


Code
# Summarise treatment adherence
pdc_adherence_result <- cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort |>
  summariseProportionOfPatientsCovered(followUpDays = 365)

library(CohortSurvival)
surv_adherence_result <- cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort |>
  summariseDiscontinuationAsSurvival()

# You can plot the results!




3.5 Step 5: Treatment switching and restart
Sometimes, one patient might switch from one treatment to another due to a lot of different causes: secondary effects, treatment failure, economic constraints, new agent introduced in the market… Independently of the reason, treatment switching and restart are valuable information to recover from the data. For our GLP-1 RA DUS, switching is particularly clinically relevant, since patients may switch between agents due to tolerability (nausea is common with all GLP-1 RAs), formulary changes, or lack of glycaemic response. A high rate of early switching (within 90 days) to a different GLP-1 RA would be a DUS finding worth reporting to regulators, as it might indicate a population-level tolerability pattern not captured in clinical trials.


Code
# Summarise switching after treatment discontinuation 
switch_result <- cdm$semaglutide_dus_cohort |>
  summariseDrugRestart(
    switchCohortTable = "GLP1-RA",
    # A cohort that you have had defined with all other GLP1-RA
    followUpDays      = 365
  )

title: Estimating effectiveness
text:
3 Example pipeline
This chapter uses a single comparative effectiveness question throughout:

Among people with T2DM who initiate semaglutide or tirzepatide, what is the comparative risk of acute pancreatitis?

The workflow is intentionally short:

Build semaglutide and tirzepatide exposure cohorts.
Intersect each exposure with T2DM.
Use the first qualifying exposure as the index date.
Exit follow-up at acute pancreatitis, death, observation end, or 3 years.
Extract baseline covariates.
Estimate propensity scores.
Match on the propensity score.
Estimate the hazard ratio with Cox regression.
Repeat with IPTW as a sensitivity analysis.
Plot Kaplan-Meier curves.
Use negative controls to assess systematic error.
Extract the final results.

CohortSurvival is used for the descriptive time-to-event/Kaplan-Meier part, while CohortMethod is used for propensity scores, matching, IPTW, and Cox regression.

3.1 Step 1: Define the study population
Our question is:

Among people with T2DM who newly start semaglutide or tirzepatide, does the risk of acute pancreatitis differ between treatments?

We use a new-user, active-comparator cohort design:

Target: semaglutide + T2DM
Comparator: tirzepatide + T2DM
Outcome: acute pancreatitis
Index date: first qualifying exposure date
Prior outcome: exclude people with previous acute pancreatitis
Follow-up: from treatment initiation until acute pancreatitis, death, the end of observation, or the end of the study risk window

The intersection with T2DM was created in the setup section. exitAtDeath() makes death an explicit censoring point for the exposure cohorts. CohortConstructor supports both cohort intersections and changing cohort end dates at death.

3.1.1 CohortSurvival
CohortSurvival can estimate Kaplan-Meier survival directly from the target and outcome cohorts. The target cohort defines who is at risk and the outcome cohort defines the event.


Code
survivalResult <- estimateSingleEventSurvival(
  cdm = cdm,
  targetCohortTable = "study_cohorts",
  outcomeCohortTable = "ap_cohort",
  outcomeWashout = Inf,       # no previous AP
  followUpDays = 1095,        # 3 years
  censorOnCohortExit = TRUE,  # includes death exit
  strata = list("cohort_definition_id")
)




3.1.2 CohortMethod
For causal estimation, CohortMethod creates the study population from the two exposure cohorts and the outcome. It can exclude people with prior outcomes and define the risk window.


Code
# Extract the data needed for CohortMethod -----------------------------
# Define which types of covariates must be constructed:
covSettings <- createDefaultCovariateSettings(
  excludedCovariateConceptIds = c(semaglutideConceptId, tirzepatideConceptId),
  addDescendantsToExclude = TRUE
)

# Load data:
cohortMethodData <- getDbCohortMethodData(
  connectionDetails = connectionDetails,
  cdmDatabaseSchema = cdmDatabaseSchema,
  targetId = 1,
  comparatorId = 2,
  outcomeIds = 4,
  exposureDatabaseSchema = cohortDatabaseSchema,
  exposureTable = cohortTable,
  outcomeDatabaseSchema = cohortDatabaseSchema,
  outcomeTable = cohortTable,
  nestingCohortDatabaseSchema = cohortDatabaseSchema,
  nestingCohortTable = cohortTable,
  getDbCohortMethodDataArgs = createGetDbCohortMethodDataArgs(
    removeDuplicateSubjects = "keep first, truncate to second",
    firstExposureOnly = TRUE,
    washoutPeriod = 365,
    restrictToCommonPeriod = TRUE,
    nestingCohortId = 3,
    covariateSettings = covSettings
  )
)
cohortMethodData

studyPop <- createStudyPopulation(
  cohortMethodData = cohortMethodData,
  removeSubjectsWithPriorOutcome = TRUE,
  minDaysAtRisk = 1,
  riskWindowStart = 0,
  startAnchor = "cohort start",
  riskWindowEnd = 1095,
  endAnchor = "cohort end"
)


For this study, baseline variables should include information such as:

age and sex
T2DM history and duration
obesity and related metabolic conditions
previous pancreatitis or pancreatic disease
gallbladder disease
alcohol-related conditions
hypertriglyceridaemia
renal disease
cardiovascular disease
diabetes medications and other relevant drugs
healthcare utilisation







Important



Simple rule for covariates: use information measured before treatment starts.





3.2 Step 2: Estimate the propensity score
The propensity score summarises the probability of receiving treatment A (semaglutide) rather than treatment B (tirzepatide), given measured baseline covariates. CohortMethod::createPs() fits the propensity model. In current versions of CohortMethod, IPTW is also derived from the propensity scores.

3.2.1 CohortSurvival
CohortSurvival uses a weight column when estimating the Kaplan-Meier curve to account for the Propensity Score, so you obtained the weighted survival directly.


Code
weightedSurvival <- estimateSingleEventSurvival(
  cdm = cdm,
  targetCohortTable = "study_cohorts",
  outcomeCohortTable = "ap_cohort",
  weight = "iptw",
  outcomeWashout = Inf,
  followUpDays = 1095,
  censorOnCohortExit = TRUE
)




3.2.2 CohortMethod


Code
ps <- createPs(
  cohortMethodData = cohortMethodData,
  population = studyPop
)

computePsAuc(ps)

plotPs(ps,
targetLabel = "semaglutide",
comparatorLabel = "tirzepatide",
showCountsLabel = TRUE,
showAucLabel = TRUE,
showEquipoiseLabel = TRUE)








Tip



Look for substantial overlap in the propensity-score distributions. Poor overlap means that some patients are very unlikely to receive one of the two treatments, so the comparison becomes dependent on extrapolation.


Quick check: If the two propensity-score distributions have almost no overlap, what problem does this create for a causal comparison?
You can do the Cox regression without adjustment for confounding because there is no confounding if the populations are too different.The causal effect estimate will be unreliable because the treatment groups are not comparable.The causal effect estimate is unreliable because the propensity scores were calculated incorrectly.



3.3 Step 3: Adjust for confounding
Here we show two simple approaches:

Propensity-score matching
Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW)


3.3.1 Propensity-score matching


Code
matchedPop <- matchOnPs(
  population = ps,
  matchOnPsArgs = createMatchOnPsArgs(
    maxRatio = 1,
    caliper = 0.2, # adjust at convenience
    caliperScale = "standardized logit"
  )
)

balance <- computeCovariateBalance(
  population = matchedPop,
  cohortMethodData = cmData
)

plotCovariateBalanceScatterPlot(
  balance,
  showMaxLabel = TRUE
)








Note



After matching, baseline covariates should be reasonably balanced between semaglutide and tirzepatide.


matchOnPs() performs propensity-score matching and removes people who cannot be matched within the specified criteria.


3.3.2 IPTW


Code
iptwPop <- truncateIptw(
  population = ps,
  truncateIptwArgs = createTruncateIptwArgs(
    maxWeight = 10
  )
)


Truncation reduces the influence of very large weights. CohortMethod supports IPTW directly in the outcome model.
Why might matching and IPTW give slightly different estimates even when both use the same propensity score?
They must produce exactly the same estimate because they use the same propensity score. TRUEFALSE
Matching focuses on creating comparable treated-control pairs, whereas IPTW uses the propensity score to weight the entire sample, so the resulting target populations can differ. TRUEFALSE
IPTW can give very large weights to patients with propensity scores near 0 or 1, while matching may exclude patients who lack suitable counterparts. TRUEFALSE
Any difference between matching and IPTW proves that the propensity-score model was incorrectly specified. TRUEFALSE



3.4 Step 4: Estimate the effect of treatment with Cox regression
The main outcome is time to first acute pancreatitis.

3.4.1 CohortMethod: Cox regression after matching


Code
outcomeModel <- fitOutcomeModel(
  population = matchedPop,
  fitOutcomeModelArgs = createFitOutcomeModelArgs(
    modelType = "cox",
    stratified = TRUE
  )
)








Note



The main result is the hazard ratio (HR) for semaglutide versus tirzepatide.

HR < 1: lower instantaneous risk with semaglutide
HR = 1: no difference
HR > 1: higher instantaneous risk with semaglutide



CohortMethod uses Cox regression for time-to-event analyses and can fit the model after propensity-score matching.


3.4.2 IPTW Cox regression


Code
iptwOutcomeModel <- fitOutcomeModel(
  population = iptwPop,
  fitOutcomeModelArgs = createFitOutcomeModelArgs(
    modelType = "cox",
    inversePtWeighting = TRUE,
    bootstrapCi = TRUE
  )
)








Important



A hazard ratio is a relative measure. It does not tell us the absolute probability of acute pancreatitis. The Kaplan-Meier analysis in the next step helps describe the absolute event experience over time.


Suppose the HR for semaglutide versus tirzepatide is 0.80 with a 95% CI of 0.60-1.07. Is it correct to say that semaglutide reduces acute pancreatitis risk?
Yes because the average effect is under 1. TRUEFALSE
No, because the confidence interval crosses 1, the threshold for signifcant difference of effect. TRUEFALSE
No, but because you need to add that reduces the comparative risk of pancreatitis. TRUEFALSE


Explanation

Although you do need to word it as “comparative risk” because you are not obtaining a measure of the absolute risk of acute pancreatitis but the comparative risk of suffering from acute pancreatitis depending on the treatment you take!




3.5 Step 5: Kaplan-Meier curves
Kaplan-Meier curves provide a simple visual description of time to acute pancreatitis.

3.5.1 CohortSurvival


Code
survivalResult <- estimateSingleEventSurvival(
  cdm = cdm,
  targetCohortTable = "study_cohorts",
  outcomeCohortTable = "ap_cohort",
  outcomeWashout = Inf,
  followUpDays = 1095,
  censorOnCohortExit = TRUE,
  strata = list("cohort_definition_id")
)

# or, as you saw before!

weightedSurvival <- estimateSingleEventSurvival(
  cdm = cdm,
  targetCohortTable = "study_cohorts",
  outcomeCohortTable = "ap_cohort",
  weight = "iptw",
  outcomeWashout = Inf,
  followUpDays = 1095,
  censorOnCohortExit = TRUE,
  strata = list("cohort_definition_id")
)


The result contains survival estimates and event information that can be used to produce Kaplan-Meier displays.






Note



CohortSurvival also supports weighting and stratification.




3.5.2 CohortMethod


Code
plotKaplanMeier(
  population = matchedPop,
  outcomeId = acutePancreatitisId,
  confidenceIntervals = TRUE
)


The two curves should be interpreted together with the Cox estimate. A small visual separation does not necessarily imply a clinically important difference.



3.6 Negative controls
A negative control is an outcome that you include in the analysis for which there is no plausible causal effect of the treatment, but which is recorded in the same healthcare data. Including negative control outcomes is good praxis to look for evidence of systematic error such as residual confounding.






Warning



Do not choose negative controls just because they are easy to find. They should be clinically unrelated to the exposure and outcome, while still being recorded often enough to be informative.




3.7 Extracting the results
The final extraction should contain only the results needed to report this study:

number of semaglutide users
number of tirzepatide users
number with acute pancreatitis
follow-up time
matched Cox HR and 95% CI
IPTW Cox HR and 95% CI
Kaplan-Meier estimates
negative-control estimates

For the survival results, CohortSurvival returns a summarised_result object that can be inspected or converted with asSurvivalResult().


Code
# Survival results
survivalTable <- asSurvivalResult(
  survivalResult
)

# Main Cox estimate
mainEstimate <- data.frame(
  analysis = "PS matched Cox",
  estimate = coef(outcomeModel),
  lower_95 = confint(outcomeModel)[1],
  upper_95 = confint(outcomeModel)[2]
)

# IPTW sensitivity estimate
iptwEstimate <- data.frame(
  analysis = "IPTW Cox",
  estimate = coef(iptwOutcomeModel),
  lower_95 = confint(iptwOutcomeModel)[1],
  upper_95 = confint(iptwOutcomeModel)[2]
)

mainEstimate
iptwEstimate
survivalTable








Tip



For a study report, keep the extraction step separate from the analysis code. This makes it easier to rerun the analysis without changing how results are reported.

4 Example pipeline
In this tutorial we will provide an example on how to run diagnostics with PhenotypeR, but further documentation can be found in the package documentation, with all available functions in its reference index and in this other tutorial.
We will see the results in a Shiny App, please, make sure that you have the necessary resources to run a shiny app in R.

4.1 1. Running PhenotypeR


Code
library(PhenotypeR)
library(here)
library(shiny)

# A folder on the local file system to store results
outputDir <- here::here("Results")

# Study parameters -----------------------------------------------------
MinCellCount <- 5 # Less than 5 counts because small numbers are a danger to privacy
if (!dir.exists(outputDir)) {
  dir.create(outputDir)
}
createLogger(outputDir, dbName)
log("Starting diagnostics")

log("Creating phenotype cohort")

cdm <- bind(cdm$semaglutide, cdm$ap_cohort, cdm$t2dm_cohort, name = "all_cohorts")

# Run phenotypeR -------------------------------------------------------
log("Running PhenotypeR")

phen_all_cohorts <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cdm$all_cohorts_table,
  diagnostics = c(
    "databaseDiagnostics",
    "codelistDiagnostics",
    "cohortDiagnostics",
    "populationDiagnostics"
  ),
  survival = TRUE,
  cohortSample = 7000, # You can adapt these numbers as you wish and depending
  matchedSample = 3000, # on your sample size
  populationSample = 1e+05
)

# Export all the results -----------------------------------------
log("Exporting results")

PhenotypeR::exportSummarisedResult(
  phen_all_cohorts,
  fileName = paste0("phenotypeR_results_{cdm_name}_{date}.csv"),
  path = outputDir,
  minCellCount = MinCellCount
)

log("Finishing diagnostics zipping results")

zip(
  zipfile = here(outputDir, paste0("phenotypeResults-", dbName, ".zip")),
  files = list.files(outputDir),
  root = outputDir
)

# To see your results in a Shiny App -----------------------
results <- omopgenerics::importSummarisedResult(
  path = here("Results"),
  # folder containing your CSV
)

PhenotypeR::shinyDiagnostics(results, directory = "Results")








Tip



When the Shiny project opens, you can run the command shiny::runApp() and the app will open on your R browser!




4.2 2. Interpreting the results

4.2.1 Cohort counts and attrition
The first diagnostic is always: how many patients are in the cohort, and how many were lost at each step?

Our study: A well-specified attrition table for the semaglutide cohort might look like this:



Step
Remaining N




Initial drug exposure records
45,210


First entry per person
12,847


≥ 365 days prior observation
11,203


No prior GLP-1 RA (washout)
9,841


T2DM diagnosis before index
8,654


Age ≥ 18
8,640


Index date 2023–2024
6,112



If the washout step removes more than 60% of patients, we need to think whether this makes sense. It may indicate that your concept set is too broad and is capturing repeat prescriptions of the same episode, or that the database has many prevalent users.

Quick check: Your attrition table shows 10,000 patients after requireIsFirstEntry() but only 200 after requirePriorDrugWashout(days = 365). What does this most likely indicate? The drug is rarely prescribed in this databaseMost drug users in this database might be prevalent users, not new usersThe washout period is too shortThe washout period is too large, we have to start by washout = 90 days


Explanation

When the vast majority of patients are excluded by the washout criterion, it means most patients who appear in the database with this drug already had prior exposure, i.e., they are prevalent users. This is common for drugs that have been on the market for many years. The new-user design deliberately excludes these patients to avoid prevalent-user bias, but it does reduce your study population substantially. This is a design trade-off, not a bug.







Important



Additionally, we need to consider the fact that we usually can only recover drug prescriptions, not the fact that the subjects in our cohort are actually taking the drug. This is constraining, and we need to bear in mind when setting a washout period the usual time between prescriptions.




4.2.2 Codelist diagnostics
The cohort code use can help us see whether relevant codes have been introduced or whether there are substances that we are including that we might want to avoid. At the same time, the orphan codes tag allows us to see potentially missed concepts that might be relevant for our study.



Figure. Code use obtained with PhenotypeR for the concepts included in a simulated type 2 diabetis mellitus cohort.








Caution



For the semaglutide exposure cohort, you expect to see Ozempic (injectable) and Rybelsus (oral) as the most used concepts. If you see unexpected concepts (which you should not because you have reviewed the list with a pharmacist, right?) your concept set needs revision.




4.2.3 Baseline and large-scale characteristics
When seeing the baseline characteristics and large-scale characteristics of your cohorts, you will be able to see whether the patients included in each cohort differ substantially between them. In our study, for example, we might see that patients receiving semaglutide and tirzepatide differ substantially. When doing the comparisons between GLP-1 RA for the safety part of our study, we need to take this into account, as it is the core confounder that we can have in our study “Are the five GLP-1 RA cohorts comparable at baseline, or do they differ systematically in ways that could explain any observed difference in pancreatitis risk?”
Large-scale characteristics are also nice because you can see the top concepts of conditions, drugs, measurements and all other domains recorded for your cohorts. If you are making a just-males cohort and you see that one of your top concepts is pregnancy, there might be something wrong with your cohort definition. You might also identify comorbidities, comedication or previous conditions that might affect the risk of your outcome of interest.






Tip



Watch out for large-scale characteristics, you might identify potential confounders!





Figure. Top concepts in a simulated type 2 diabetis mellitus cohort obtained from the large-scale characterisation section of PhenotypeR.




4.2.4 Cohort overlap
High overlap between exposure cohorts when you do not expect that could mean that your cohort exit criteria are not correctly excluding patients who switch between agents. For example, if a patient switches from liraglutide to semaglutide, they should exit the liraglutide cohort at the switch date and enter the semaglutide cohort. Failure to handle this correctly leads to immortal time and misclassification bias.

title: Characterisation
text:
3 Example pipeline
In this tutorial we will provide an example on how to do a descriptive/characterisation study with CohortCharacteristics, but further documentation can be found in the package documentation, with all available functions in its reference index and in this other tutorial.

3.1 Cohort counts


Code
counts <- summariseCohortCount(cdm$study_cohorts)
tableCohortCount(counts)




3.2 Basic demographics


Code
resultsBlc <- summariseCharacteristics(
  cohort   = cdm$study_cohorts,
  ageGroup = list(c(18, 44), c(45, 64), c(65, 150))
)




3.3 Large-scale characteristics
Large-scale characterisation reports the prevalence of every domain (condition, drug, procedure…) in a specified time window around the index date. This produces potentially thousands of features. We can also look for the most common ones in our cohorts!


Code
resultsLsc <- cdm$study_cohorts |>
  summariseLargeScaleCharacteristics(
    window           = list(c(-365, -1), c(0, 0), c(1, 30)), # We usually add multiple time windows in which to assess ls characteristics
    eventInWindow    = c("condition_occurrence", "drug_exposure"), # You can add all desired domains
    minimumFrequency = 0.01
  )








NoteWhy those time windows?




c(-365, -1) or the year prior to index: captures baseline comorbidities and prior medications (covariates for confounding adjustment)
c(0, 0) or the index date itself: captures what was coded at the time of drug initiation (the index event breakdown)
c(1, 30) or the 30 days after index: captures early treatment patterns and complications (not used for baseline characterisation, but useful for drug utilisation analyses)





3.4 Comparing cohorts: the standardised mean difference
When the goal is to compare two cohorts (as in our head-to-head GLP-1 RA safety study), we compute the standardised mean difference (SMD)1 for each covariate. Any covariate with SMD \(\ge\) 0.1 is a candidate for inclusion in the propensity score model. We can do this with the CohortCharacterisation package using the compared large scale characterisation.


Code
resultsSmd <- resultsLsc |>
  plotComparedLargeScaleCharacteristics(
    reference = "semaglutide",
    colour    = "variable_level"
  )


Let’s do a quick check now!
Quick check: You are characterising the five GLP-1 RA cohorts. You find that 28% of exenatide users have a prior record of cholelithiasis compared to 11% of semaglutide users. This is an SMD of 0.47. What should you do?
Borderline, can be ignored if the outcome is not hepatobiliaryBorderline, adjust in the outcome model onlySLarge imbalance, include cholelithiasis in the propensity score model since it is a strong confounder for APLarge imbalance, exclude all patients with cholelithiasis from both cohorts


Explanation

The SMD ≈ 0.47, this is a large imbalance. Since cholelithiasis (gallstones) is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide, this is a strong confounder, because not only it is differentially distributed between the cohorts but also directly causes the outcome. It must be included in the propensity score model. Excluding patients with cholelithiasis would change the target population and invalidate generalisation of the results.



3.5 Cohort overlap


Code
resultsOverlap <- summariseCohortOverlap(cdm$study_cohorts)

title: Study Outline
text:
2 Why a study outline?
You might wonder: why invest time in a structured study outline if this document is never going to be published? The answer lies in two practical realities of multi-partner research.
First, the process of writing a study outline forces collaboration. When researchers sit down to define the population, the exposure, the outcome, the comparator, and all different parts of the study they want to suggest, gaps in knowledge surface immediately. Some investigators may have strong clinical expertise but limited familiarity with how the condition is coded in electronic health records. Others may know the data well but lack the clinical context to judge which outcomes are meaningful. And others may flag that the proposed washout period is inconsistent with the prescribing patterns they observe in their database. None of these caveats could be overcome if each team worked in isolation, so making them become visible enforces a study team to work collaboratively with the rest of the network, with the aim that the study elements are written down explicitly and reviewed collectively. The study outline is, in this sense, less a document than a structured conversation.
Second, the study outline is the foundation of the feasibility assessment. Before you can ask whether your data can support a study, you need to know precisely what study you are trying to run. Defining the study elements first is what makes the subsequent steps possible.
